Rebuttal:
Response to Reviewer Pm4m

We thank the reviewer for the careful, constructive review, for the close reading down to the router parameter count and α initialization, and for noting that addressing these concerns would raise the score. We address every point below; all supporting results are in the submitted paper unless tagged [NEW].

W1 (framing / DLinear). (Meta-review point 1: "overstate of claims in the paper and requires reframing of contributions.") This is the reviewer's central concern, and we take it seriously. The reviewer is correct that our abstract's headline numbers (54/54; 12-79% over full fine-tuning) are all comparisons within the frozen-adapter/PEFT regime. Those are the right baselines for the frozen-adapter question we ask, and we agree a from-scratch DLinear belongs beside them as a benchmark from outside that regime. Against that benchmark, the reviewer's point holds for RR-MoA-proper: it does trail a from-scratch DLinear on linear-dominated data (~0.68 vs ~0.42 on ETTh1, exactly as noted), because the probe's role is to isolate the router input, not chase accuracy. The variant we deploy differs. Residual-IA+, reported in the submitted Appendix P, matches or beats DLinear rather than trailing it:

65 significant wins vs 11 losses (5.9:1); 107/123 match-or-beat (87%) across 6 backbones × 6 datasets × 4 horizons.
6/6 at H=192; MOMENT-large 23/24 with zero losses (16 significant wins); Moirai-MoE 15/15 (100%).
It dominates non-stationary data at long horizons (ETTm2 -27.0% at H=720; ETTh2 wins at all four).
Even at the single least-favorable case cited (MOMENT-small, H=96), the net mean gap is -2.8%, a win, with ETTh1 the only loss.
We acknowledge that the reviewer is right about our framing; the issue is how we presented the evidence, not the evidence itself. We led with "5/6 match-or-beat" and titled the appendix "Closing the DLinear Gap," which highlighted the single losing cell (ETTh1/H=96). We will fix the presentation in three ways:

Promote the full grid, the 65:11 win-count, and the backbone-contribution analysis (App. P.3) into the main text, as the reviewer asks.
Retitle the section to the outperformance the numbers actually show.
Reframe the abstract's DLinear comparison as a matter of scope, not a weakness, with wording such as: "Because the router isolates the collapse mechanism rather than maximizing accuracy, the minimal RR-MoA probe trails a from-scratch DLinear on linear-dominated datasets; our deployment adapter Residual-IA+ removes this gap, matching or beating DLinear across six backbones and four horizons."
We will present RR-MoA-proper as a diagnostic probe and Residual-IA+ as the deployed method that clears the DLinear bar; the overselling concern is thus one of framing, which we fix.

W2 (Figure 2). We agree the figure is too small and cluttered; we will redraw it larger with non-overlapping modules so it clearly shows the raw-router and frozen-expert paths.

W3 (Moirai gains without collapse). The reviewer is right, and we should have made this clearer. On Moirai there is no collapse, so its 12-29% gain is not collapse-repair. We read it as two results. (1) It confirms the prediction: Moirai has no learnable-affine input normalization, so the co-adaptation that drives collapse cannot occur. (2) Raw routing still helps, for a different reason: Moirai's non-learnable normalization (Kim et al. 2022) also strips per-window location-scale from the hidden states, and the raw input lets the router recover it, a routing effect, not the raw-signal predictiveness the reviewer links to App. P.3: in RR-MoA the raw signal feeds only the router, and experts use frozen hidden states. So the gain cannot come from the Pure Raw-MLP mechanism, where experts read the raw signal directly. So the cross-backbone wins split into two regimes the diagnosis predicts: collapse-repair on learnable-affine RevIN backbones, routing-signal recovery elsewhere. That is a sharper claim than uniform collapse-repair, not a weaker one; the causal chain stands, and we will add the Moirai citation.

W4 (heavy tuning; generalization beyond six). We appreciate this careful read, and believe both concerns have direct answers: the recipe is fixed once and generalizes to unseen data without re-tuning, and the backbone's value is horizon-dependent, near-negligible at H=96 but decisive at H≥192. On the tuning, the 546-run sweep (Appendix P) was a one-time search for one fixed recipe, not a per-dataset cost, so it should not read as a SOTA search, and it gives a win over DLinear (65:11) rather than parity. [NEW] When we apply that recipe unchanged (gate-init b=-2, 5-epoch warmup, shared NLinear, validation early-stop) to three unseen datasets, Residual-IA+ matches or beats DLinear on 8 of 9 cells (Solar 3/3, -9.5%; Traffic 3/3, parity; Exchange 2/3; no collapse).

The reviewer reads App. P.3 as "the raw branch does the work; the TSFM is dead weight," and at H=96 the paper largely agrees: there the backbone's contribution is dataset-dependent and negligible on average. But two things undercut that verdict for the deployed model. First, P.3 measures it against the intermediate Dual-Stream (ETTh2 0.452, ETTm2 0.252), not the deployed Residual-IA+ (ETTh2 0.346, ETTm2 0.188). Second, it is an artifact of the short horizon. [NEW] At H=192, holding the raw branch fixed and toggling only the backbone, the verdict flips outright: Residual-IA+ wins 18/18 (mean -11.8%) on the very ETTh2/ETTm2/Electricity cells P.3 called dead-weight, and still matches or beats a 49K DLinear. So the backbone is not dead weight; at H≥192 it is decisive.

W5 ((μ,σ) tension). (Meta-review point 2: "the (M,Σ)-centric quantity contradicts with paper's ablations.") We understand why this looks like a contradiction; it dissolves once we separate what the router reads from what normalization removes. Normalization is by definition a per-window location-scale map, so it removes exactly (M,Σ); Observation 1 and R(D) are therefore (M,Σ)-centric by necessity, and never claim (M,Σ) is the whole routing signal. R(D) is a ratio: routing signal in the removed part (location-scale) over routing signal in the surviving part (shape). The reviewer's two ablations are exactly that denominator: [μ,σ]-only routing degrades +48% because it drops the surviving shape, and temporal shuffling barely moves performance (≤3% on 4/6, the rest improve) because the signal is order-invariant shape, what normalization leaves. Both populate the denominator, not contradict the numerator. So the theory matches the data: collapse at high R(D), none at low (Traffic R=0.14, where RR-MoA correctly does not improve). We will re-scope Observation 1 as a lower-bound vulnerability predictor, not a claim that (μ,σ) alone is enough.

W6 (minor). The router is 853 params for the reported K=5 model, consistent across the main text, Fig 2, Table A.1, and the code. The K-way head grows with K, so over the expert-count sweep (Table I.3, to K=10) the count reaches 1,100; the Checklist's "1.1K" reflects that larger-K count, not the reported K=5, and we will correct it to 853. On the SR-MoA figure, the 13-42% is over RR-MoA, not the baselines (SR-MoA beats RR-MoA on all six, Table F.2). We will standardize "fine-tuning" and recheck the flagged R(D) parenthesis.

Q1 (input length 512 / horizon 96). The input length is indeed fixed at 512, and the reviewer is right to question it. Multi-horizon results, though, are already in the submitted paper (Table C.1: RR-MoA 12/12 vs best fixed over H∈{96,192,336,720}; Residual-IA+ reaches 6/6 at H=192 in Table P.6); we may not have presented them prominently enough. [NEW] Input-length ablation (L∈{96,192,336,512}, 6 datasets, 3 seeds): no collapse at any L (per-seed entropy 0.89-1.53, far above the 0.00 collapse floor), raw beats normalized routing at all 24 configs (-17% to -84%), and RR-MoA beats the best fixed adapter at 70/72. The answer is yes: both the method and its conclusions hold as the input length and the forecast horizon change, not only at L=512 and H=96.

Routing entropy per seed (each cell = seeds 42/43/44; H=96):

dataset    L=96    L=192    L=336    L=512
ETTh1    1.31/1.39/1.39    1.41/1.48/1.42    1.46/1.51/1.46    1.45/1.45/1.49
ETTh2    1.19/1.23/1.28    1.28/1.16/1.17    1.32/1.06/0.92    0.92/0.89/1.13
ETTm1    1.34/1.39/1.45    1.36/1.42/1.39    1.25/1.52/1.39    1.48/1.46/1.37
ETTm2    1.16/1.31/1.26    1.12/1.22/1.14    1.16/1.13/1.23    1.21/1.26/1.08
Electricity    1.40/1.38/1.44    1.53/1.44/1.43    1.48/1.48/1.38    1.50/1.48/1.40
Weather    1.47/1.46/1.47    1.37/1.41/1.46    1.37/1.32/1.42    1.47/1.44/1.30
Q2 (α inconsistency). Thank you for catching this; it is a wording slip. α is initialized at σ(0)=0.5 (the logit is a parameter at 0.0); 0.492 is the mean α at the end of the first logged epoch, after one epoch has moved it below 0.5, not the initialization (trajectory 0.5 → 0.492 → 0.468). We will correct the wording.

On significance. The lasting contribution is the diagnosis and its predictor. R(D) is a practical, training-free tool: computed before training, it predicts whether raw routing will help on a new dataset (ρ=-0.88, n=9), and where it will not (Traffic, R=0.14). It transfers beyond our six benchmarks and our router: two distinct variants (SR-MoA, Residual-IA+) confirm it.

We report per-seed results here for length; full tables will follow in the revision if accepted. Given the corrected DLinear framing (Residual-IA+ beats DLinear 65:11, App. P), the re-scoped R(D), and the new input-length ablation, which the reviewer noted would raise the score, we would be grateful for a reconsideration."

Response to Authors
I thank the authors for the detailed rebuttal and the new experiments. The minor issues (router parameter count, α initialization, Figure 2, line 64) are resolved However, two substantive issues remain (W3 and W4), and in both cases the rebuttal contradicts either the paper itself or leaves the decisive control missing. My reasons are as follows.

1. The rebuttal's explanation of the Moirai gains contradicts the paper itself
The paper, §4.1 (lines 188–190), states that non-learnable I/O scaling "preserves the (M, Σ) statistics in the hidden states the router reads". This is the stated reason regime (ii) is not vulnerable. The rebuttal's response to my W3 asserts the opposite: Moirai's non-learnable normalization "also strips per-window location-scale from the hidden states, and the raw input lets the router recover it." The rebuttal presents the reversal as "a sharper claim, not a weaker one" without acknowledging that it rewrites the paper's stated mechanism. Table N.2's caption meanwhile hedges in the original direction ("hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse"), and the rule offered to Reviewer 8b2Z ("a normalizer causes collapse when it strips routing-relevant statistics at the router's input") silently replaces the paper's learnable-affine criterion.

Which claim is correct?

2. "Residual-IA+ matches or beats DLinear" is confounded by NLinear vs. a simplified DLinear
Two facts from the submission itself: Residual-IA+'s shared raw branch is NLinear (App. P.1, fix (v): y = Linear(x − x_T) + x_T), while the calibration anchor is the simplified single-Linear DLinear without trend-seasonal decomposition (App. A, lines 640–643). NLinear's from-scratch advantage over DLinear on level-drifting data is a known result from [17] itself, and the paper's own Batch-4 analysis (lines 1309–1315) shows the same pattern inside the adapter: the NLinear branch helps most on precisely the non-stationary ETT datasets, "matching NLinear's design rationale."

The headline defense of W1/W4 (65 significant wins vs. 11 losses) therefore compares a method whose base predictor is a stronger linear model against a weaker linear anchor. As reported, the grid cannot distinguish "the backbone adds value" from "NLinear beats a simplified DLinear." The [NEW] Exchange result (a ~10× RR-MoA deficit in Table N.4 flipping to 2/3 match-or-beat) is exactly what level anchoring predicts on near-random-walk data, backbone or not. Add a variant from-scratch NLinear, trained under the same protocol as the DLinear anchor would be persuasive."""

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for a second careful reading. Setting the two quotations side by side was the right check. We settle the first below; the second names the right control for the anchor question, which we have run.

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's.**

We clarify that the paper's claim is correct and consistent on this point, as is the rule we gave Reviewer 8b2Z. We can see why the two read as a reversal, though, and the confusion is ours. One clause in our W3 answer described what normalization does to its **input**, but phrased it as a claim about the **representation** the encoder builds. Next to §4.1 it could hardly read otherwise.

We should say how it happened. The reviewer asked why raw routing helps on a backbone that does not collapse, reading the gain as App. P.3's raw-signal predictiveness. We wanted to show it was a routing effect instead. Per-instance scaling subtracts each window's mean and divides by its scale, so the encoder never sees the location-scale, and we assumed the same for the router without checking. The two-regime reading is genuinely sharper, but we should have said clearly that we were also rewording the mechanism.

We have since measured it, taking the tensor a hidden-state router reads and recovering each window's mean. On Moirai the mean is recoverable (R²=0.996); on MOMENT under RevIN it is not (−0.311). Switching RevIN off restores it to 0.999, showing the probe works. The statistics are present in what the router reads, which is §4.1's claim. What we measured is decodability there, not the scaling mechanism. The account we should have given was already in Table N.2's caption: raw-signal routing is information-richer than hidden-state routing *even when the hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse*. Nothing need go missing for the gain to be a routing effect.

That clause aside, the rest of our W3 answer stands. There is no collapse on Moirai, so the gain is not collapse-repair. Nor can it be App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect: in RR-MoA the raw signal reaches only the router, while experts read frozen hidden states. The rule we gave 8b2Z was shorthand for the same criterion; both give the same verdict on every App. H case: collapse needs the statistics removed from what the router reads **and** a learnable affine map that can co-adapt (Prop. 1). Moirai has neither, so those passages are one account, not three.

**2. The NLinear control: NLinear is the stronger anchor on three of nine datasets.**

We are convinced that both facts cited are correct, and that the proposed control is the right test of the anchor effect, so we have run it: a from-scratch NLinear under the DLinear anchor's protocol (Linear(512→96), 49K, same optimizer and schedule), differing only by the level anchor, n=10. Our DLinear reproduces the published anchor on all six (ETTh1 0.4187 vs 0.419±0.005), as does Residual-IA+, so the comparison uses the paper's baseline. The control does separate the anchor effect from the rest: level anchoring explains the margin where the level drifts, and elsewhere the margin survives the stronger anchor.

We agree the effect is real, and can say how far it reaches. Across nine datasets at n=10, NLinear beats DLinear on three, all with drifting levels: Exchange (−28.9%), ETTh2 (−3.8%, −19.0% at H=192) and ETTm2 (−7.9%). On the other six it is equal or worse, losing 0/10 seeds on Traffic. DLinear is more often the stronger anchor, so the swap does not favour one side.

At H=96, n=10, Residual-IA+ is **5/6** against each anchor, ETTm1 within 0.1% of NLinear (ETTh1 loses to DLinear, ETTh2 to NLinear): the swap changes which dataset fails, not how many. On Weather and Electricity, where the anchor does not help, it beats both on 9 of 10.

Beyond the six, on datasets never used to build the recipe, Solar wins 20 of 20 against the stronger anchor (−8.7%, −11.2%), Traffic 15/20 at −0.3% and −0.9%, as R(D)=0.14 predicts. We agree with the reviewer on Exchange: the −26.3% over DLinear is accounted for by level anchoring alone, on data close to a random walk. Against NLinear it is at parity at H=96 and behind at H=192, so we now read it as parity.

One further consequence follows. Residual-IA+ is a shared NLinear branch plus a gated backbone residual. Close the gate and what remains is this anchor. The two therefore differ only in the backbone path, so the comparison above is also a backbone control: the backbone earns its place on 5 of 6 datasets, and on 9 of 10 cells where anchoring adds nothing. Our first response cited the backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE instead (18 of 18 at H=192). That model swaps the raw branch for an MLP as well, so it cannot separate the two effects, and the matched anchor is the better evidence.

These results are MOMENT-small, and the 65:11 count is a DLinear comparison. We are extending the anchor to the other backbones, a good addition we owe to this exchange.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

 **1. Which claim is correct: the paper's.**
 
@@ -10,18 +10,18 @@ We should say how it happened. The reviewer asked why raw routing helps on a bac
 
 We have since measured it, taking the tensor a hidden-state router reads and recovering each window's mean. On Moirai the mean is recoverable (R²=0.996); on MOMENT under RevIN it is not (−0.311). Switching RevIN off restores it to 0.999, showing the probe works. The statistics are present in what the router reads, which is §4.1's claim. What we measured is decodability there, not the scaling mechanism. The account we should have given was already in Table N.2's caption: raw-signal routing is information-richer than hidden-state routing *even when the hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse*. Nothing need go missing for the gain to be a routing effect.

Nor can it be App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect: in RR-MoA the raw signal reaches only the router, while experts read frozen hidden states. The rule we gave 8b2Z was shorthand for the same criterion; both give the same verdict on every App. H case: collapse needs the statistics removed from what the router reads **and** a learnable affine map that can co-adapt (Prop. 1). Moirai has neither, so those passages are one account, not three.
 
 **2. The NLinear control: NLinear is the stronger anchor on three of nine datasets.**
 
 We are convinced that both facts cited are correct, and that the proposed control is the right test of the anchor effect, so we have run it: a from-scratch NLinear under the DLinear anchor's protocol (Linear(512→96), 49K, same optimizer and schedule), differing only by the level anchor, n=10. Our DLinear reproduces the published anchor on all six (ETTh1 0.4187 vs 0.419±0.005), as does Residual-IA+, so the comparison uses the paper's baseline. The control does separate the anchor effect from the rest: level anchoring explains the margin where the level drifts, and elsewhere the margin survives the stronger anchor.
 
-We agree the effect is real, and can say how far it reaches. Across nine datasets at n=10, NLinear beats DLinear on three, all with drifting levels: Exchange (−28.9%), ETTh2 (−3.8%, −19.0% at H=192) and ETTm2 (−7.9%). On the other six it is equal or worse, losing 0/10 seeds on Traffic. DLinear is more often the stronger anchor, so the swap does not favour one side.
 
-At H=96, n=10, Residual-IA+ is **5/6** against each anchor, ETTm1 within 0.1% of NLinear (ETTh1 loses to DLinear, ETTh2 to NLinear): changing the anchor changes which dataset fails, not how many. On Weather and Electricity, where the anchor does not help, it beats both on 9 of 10.
+At H=96, n=10, Residual-IA+ is **5/6** against each anchor, ETTm1 within 0.1% of NLinear (ETTh1 loses to DLinear, ETTh2 to NLinear): the swap changes which dataset fails, not how many. On Weather and Electricity, where the anchor does not help, it beats both on 9 of 10.
 
-Beyond the six, on datasets never used to build the recipe, Solar wins 20 of 20 against the stronger anchor (−8.7% and −11.2%), and Traffic 15/20 at −0.3% and −0.9%, as R(D)=0.14 predicts. We agree with the reviewer on Exchange: the −26.3% over DLinear is accounted for by level anchoring alone, on data close to a random walk where the last value is near the best predictor. Against NLinear it is at parity at H=96 and behind at H=192, so we now read it as parity.
+Beyond the six, on datasets never used to build the recipe, Solar wins 20 of 20 against the stronger anchor (−8.7%, −11.2%), Traffic 15/20 at −0.3% and −0.9%, as R(D)=0.14 predicts. We agree with the reviewer on Exchange: the −26.3% over DLinear is accounted for by level anchoring alone, on data close to a random walk. Against NLinear it is at parity at H=96 and behind at H=192, so we now read it as parity.
 
-Beating NLinear does not by itself isolate the backbone from routing or the residual path. A backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE does lose to Residual-IA+ on 18 of 18 cells at H=192 (mean −11.8%), on the cells App. P.3 called negligible, but its raw branch is an MLP rather than our NLinear, so it does not isolate the backbone either; our first response called it a backbone toggle, which was imprecise. A control varying only that path would, and that is future work.
+One further consequence follows. Residual-IA+ is a shared NLinear branch plus a gated backbone residual. Close the gate and what remains is this anchor. The two therefore differ only in the backbone path, so the comparison above is also a backbone control: the backbone earns its place on 5 of 6 datasets, and on 9 of 10 cells where anchoring adds nothing. Our first response cited the backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE instead (18 of 18 at H=192). That model swaps the raw branch for an MLP as well, so it cannot separate the two effects, and the matched anchor is the better evidence.
 
 These results are MOMENT-small, and the 65:11 count is a DLinear comparison. We are extending the anchor to the other backbones, a good addition we owe to this exchange.

410:\textbf{Backbones.} We use six backbones spanning three normalization regimes: (i)~learnable-affine RevIN-inside-encoder MOMENT-small/large~\citep{goswami2024moment} (internal RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin}); (ii)~Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} and Moirai-MoE, which use RMSNorm internally with only non-learnable per-instance I/O scaling (no learnable-affine RevIN inside the encoder pipeline); (iii)~Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos} (T5-style, no instance normalization) and Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl} (LayerNorm only, no instance normalization) as no-instance-normalization negative controls (per-backbone normalization specifications in Appendix~\ref{app:setup}; full cross-backbone results in App.~\ref{app:cross_backbone}). MOMENT-small is primary. Primary results use a strictly frozen backbone; freeze-level ablations follow.

I've completed the audit. Here are the findings.

## VERDICT

**Section 1 is not defensible as written.** Its central sentence — *"both give the same verdict on every App. H case: collapse needs the statistics removed from what the router reads **and** a learnable affine map that can co-adapt (Prop. 1)"* (reply line 13) — is falsified by two cases inside Appendix H itself, mis-cites Prop. 1, and contradicts what we told the AC. Sections 1's *position* (the paper's claim is right, our W3 clause was the error) is correct and defensible; the *argument* offered for it is not.

---

## CRITICAL

### F1. The conjunctive rule is falsified by App. H.1, case E — and the two rules give **opposite** verdicts there

`main.tex:1972` (Table H.2, `tab:vision_moe`):
```
\multirow{2}{*}{ViT-B/16} & E & Frozen + InstanceNorm1d & $\mathbf{0.000 \pm 0.000}$ & \textbf{Yes} & $0.953$
```
Verified in code: `scripts/run_vision_moe_vit_collapse.py:168` → `self.norm = nn.InstanceNorm1d(d_model, affine=False)`; `:393-397` → `"E_frozen_instancenorm": {"frozen": True, ...}`; the router reads `normed[:, 0]` directly (`:220`), so there is **no trainable map anywhere between the normalizer and the router**.

- Reply's rule (statistics removed **AND** learnable affine that can co-adapt) → predicts **no collapse**. Actual: **0.000, full collapse**. ✗
- 8b2Z rule ("strips routing-relevant statistics at the router's input") → predicts **collapse**. ✓

This is the exact opposite of "both give the same verdict on every App. H case", and the rule that fails is the one the reply is defending. If Pm4m checks Appendix H (which they were already reading), section 1 is dead.

### F2. App. H.1 case C: collapse with **no normalizer at all** — falsifies the necessity direction of both rules

`main.tex:1969` and `:1978`:
```
& C & Unfrozen + No norm & $\mathbf{0.184 \pm 0.260}$ & \textbf{Yes} & $0.921$
```

Confirmed against App. P.3: the Raw-MLP MoE replaces the raw branch with "$K{=}5$ size-diverse two-layer MLPs... $\text{Linear}(512{\to}h_k) \to \text{GELU} \to \text{Linear}(h_k{\to}96)$" (`main.tex:2840`). Calling this "imprecise" understates a factual retraction; a reviewer already hunting for contradictions will score it as a second one. Recommend stating plainly that the round-1 sentence was wrong.

---

## MEDIUM

### F9. Table N.2's caption says what the reply quotes — but its own explanation cuts against the use

Question C: **yes, verbatim.** `main.tex:2216`, final clause:
> "...consistent with raw-signal routing being information-richer than hidden-state routing **even when the hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse**."

Two problems. (a) It is **Moirai-MoE**, not Moirai; the reply's W3 subject is Moirai's 12–29%. (b) The same caption gives a *different* reason for the non-collapse: "under a strictly frozen backbone **the router-input gradient is dominated by the load-balance term and the softmax saturates at uniform mixing**, so routing entropy hovers at $\log K = 1.6094$ to four decimal places across all 30 cells ($\sigma{=}0.0000$, indicating **mathematically uniform rather than specialized routing**)." A router pinned at exactly uniform is not using the retained statistics at all, so "the hidden states retain enough signal" is the caption's *conclusion*, not its mechanism. Quoting only the last clause is fair but fragile.

### F10. §4.1's causal half is not vindicated by the probe (question D)

`main.tex:410`, exact:
> "The collapse mechanism predicts that only regime~(i) is vulnerable: routing signal is destroyed by RevIN's learnable-affine normalization upstream of the encoder, whereas **non-learnable I/O scaling preserves the (M,$\Sigma$) statistics in the hidden states the router reads**."

The probe reads exactly the right tensor — `stat_decodability_core.py:78` "*Exactly the router's input: last-block hidden states, mean-pooled*", matching AdaMix's router (`main.tex:1893`, "a single linear layer $\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^K$ operating on the mean-pooled hidden state"). So the reply's "decodability there, not the scaling mechanism" distinction is **coherent**, and §4.1's *outcome* claim is a presence claim that decodability confirms. But §4.1 also asserts the *cause* ("non-learnable I/O scaling preserves"), and the reply concedes that reasoning is wrong (line 9) — compounded by F5, where the scaling never ran. So "the paper's claim is correct" (line 7) is true of half of §4.1's sentence. Say which half.

### F11. Section 2's NLinear/dataset claims sit awkwardly next to Batch 4

Reply line 19: *"On the other six it is equal or worse."* Batch 4 (`main.tex:2646`) reports the NLinear raw branch **improving** Weather ($-6.6\% \to -8.7\%$) and ETTh1 ($+5.1\% \to +3.3\%$). Different comparisons (standalone anchor vs raw branch inside Residual-IA), but the reviewer has just been directed to Batch 4. One clause of disambiguation is cheap insurance.

---

## LOW

### F12. Round-1 mis-attributed Moirai's normalization
`response_pm4m.md:22`: "Moirai's non-learnable normalization **(Kim et al. 2022)**" — Kim et al. is the RevIN paper (`main.tex:410` cites it as `kim2021revin`, 2021); Moirai is `woo2024moirai`. Not addressed in round 2.

### F13. Traffic weakened between rounds
Round-1 (`response_pm4m.md:24`): "Traffic 3/3, parity". Round-2 (line 23): "Traffic 15/20 at $-0.3\%$ and $-0.9\%$". Same dataset, 3/3 → 15/20.

---

## Direct answers

**A.** §4.1 (`main.tex:410`) and the intro (`main.tex:68`, "narrowing the cause to learnable-affine encoder normalization") do state a learnable-affine criterion — so the reply's position is *supportable*. But the paper does **not** state it as a conjunction with Prop. 1, and it states a **weaker, overlap-only criterion in four other places** (F6). Prop. 1 (`main.tex:500-503`) requires a trainable **backbone**, not an affine normalizer (F4).

**B.** **Not equivalent — the reply is papering over a real difference.** Full App. H verdict table:

| Case | main.tex | Actual | Reply's rule | 8b2Z rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RevIN (affine) | 1942 | 0.507→0.000 Yes | ✓ | ✓ |
| BatchNorm1d (`nn.BatchNorm1d(1)`, affine=True) | 1943 | 0.619→0.004 Yes | ✓ | ✓ |
| GroupNorm (`nn.GroupNorm(1,1)`, affine=True) | 1944 | 0.507→0.000 Yes | ✓ | ✓ |
| None (identity) | 1946 | 0.623→0.817 No | ✓ | ✓ |
| [NEW] input-position LayerNorm (affine=True) | — | →0.000 Yes | ✓ | ✓ |
| A ResNet unfrozen + IN2d | 1967 | 1.475 No | ✓* | ✓* |
| B ResNet frozen + IN2d | 1968 | 0.992 No | ✓ | ✓ |
| **C ResNet unfrozen + no norm** | 1969 | **0.184 Yes** | **✗** | **✗** |
| D ResNet unfrozen + BN2d | 1970 | 1.476 No | ✓* | ✓* |
| **E ViT frozen + IN1d (affine=False)** | 1972 | **0.000 Yes** | **✗** | **✓** |
| F ViT frozen + no norm | 1973 | 0.494 No | ✓ | ✓ |

\* only under the "routing-**relevant**" wording of `response_8b2z.md:45`; the `discussion_8b2z.md:21` wording ("strips per-window statistics") gets A, B, D wrong. **Case E is the critical divergence.**

**C.** Yes, verbatim (`main.tex:2216`) — with the caveats in F9.

**D.** Coherent; the probe reads the correct tensor. §4.1 claims *preservation in the hidden states* (a presence claim), which decodability establishes. But §4.1 also claims a cause, which the reply concedes and F5 undermines.

**E.** `main.tex:2551`: "*Stream 2* (green): **a shared NLinear branch reads $\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw}$ directly, producing $\mathbf{y}_\mathrm{raw}$ — DLinear-equivalent and shared across all $K$ experts. Each expert combines them as $\mathbf{y}_k = \mathbf{y}_\mathrm{raw} + \sigma(\mathrm{blend}_k(\mathbf{X}_\mathrm{raw})) \cdot \mathrm{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$, with the blend gate initialized at $b{=}{-}2$**". Also `main.tex:2811`: "$\mathbf{y}_k = \text{NLinear}(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}) + \sigma(\text{blend}_k(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})) \cdot \text{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H})$". Fixes: (i) residual formulation, (ii) gate-init $b{=}{-}2$, (iii) 5-epoch raw warmup, **(iv) shared raw branch, (v) NLinear raw architecture $\mathbf{y} = \text{Linear}(\mathbf{x} - x_T) + x_T$, (vi) validation early stopping** — six, not five; NLinear is (v). Architecturally, closing the gate does leave exactly $\mathbf{y}_\mathrm{raw}$ (weights sum to 1 over a shared branch). **Training-wise it does not** — see F7.

**F.** Reviewer is exactly right. `main.tex:1203`: "we use the **simplified single-Linear variant** ($\text{Linear}(L{=}512 \to H{=}96)$, $49$K params), **without the trend-seasonal decomposition**, as the calibration anchor."

**G.** Batch 4 is at `main.tex:2646`, not 1309-1315 (those lines are the Observation-1 MI proof). Quote: "Testing `--raw-arch nlinear` as a drop-in replacement reduces ETTh1 from $+5.1\%$ to $+3.3\%$ and ETTh2 from $+10.6\%$ to $+6.9\%$ at $n{=}3$ seeds, while *improving* (not regressing) ETTm2 ($-1.6\% \to -4.1\%$) and Weather ($-6.6\% \to -8.7\%$). **The improvement is largest where non-stationarity is most pronounced**". The reviewer is **substantially but not exactly** right: NLinear helps on all four tested, Weather (non-ETT) gains more than ETTh1, and `main.tex:2650` notes "NLinear improves the ETTh pair but **regresses ETTm1**".

**H.** Yes — F3 (AC), plus the F4 tension with `response_8b2z.md:55` (frozen MOMENT called "near-collapse" at 0.49). No contradiction found with `response_jemj.md`.

**I.** No. Round-1 (`response_pm4m.md:26`) explicitly claimed "**holding the raw branch fixed and toggling only the backbone**" — a factual assertion the reply now negates, not a framing choice. See F8.

---

## Recommended repair to section 1 (minimum viable)

1. Delete "both give the same verdict on every App. H case" and the "(Prop. 1)" citation.
2. Replace with the paper's own unifying principle (`main.tex:1982` / `:658`) and say plainly: the paper states an overlap criterion (App. H, Conclusion) and a learnable-affine *narrowing* for the TSFM regime (§4.1, intro); the 8b2Z rule is the former, verbatim from Appendix H, not a substitute for it. Concede that ViT-E (frozen, `affine=False`, collapses) shows the affine clause is not necessary — it describes regime (i), it is not the general law.
3. Resolve F5 before posting, or drop the "Per-instance scaling... the encoder never sees the location-scale" sentence entirely — it is the sentence that makes R²=0.996 look impossible.
4. Drop "differ only in the backbone path" (F7) or qualify it to "differ in the backbone path, with the anchor trained under its own published protocol."

Schedule and capacity differ, not only the backbone path.

5. **Several stated wins are not significant.** ETTh2's "NLinear beats DLinear −3.8%" at H=96 is p=0.127 (H=192 −19.0% is p=0.008). Traffic's "15/20" includes H=96 at p=0.53 (6/10 seeds), which is a tie, not a win — though the reply's framing ("as R(D)=0.14 predicts") is consistent with the paper's own "statistically indistinguishable" wording. Exchange "behind at H=192" (+11.06%) is p=0.33.

6. **Two numbers have no archived artifact.** Traffic R(D)=0.14 is absent from `results/analysis/routing_signal_ratio.json` (8 datasets, Traffic missing, and only 5 have a `delta_pct`, versus the paper's n=9 ρ=−0.88); I reproduced 0.1353 from `data/traffic.csv`. And no anchor result file records which backbone was used, so "These results are MOMENT-small" rests on the script default and directory naming.

## n / horizons / testing basis

- **n=10 seeds (42–51)** for everything cited in section 2: `linear_anchors` (9 datasets × H∈{96,192}), `nlinear_anchor_h96` (6 datasets), `offsuite_anchor_h{96,192}` (Exchange/Solar/Traffic). `nlinear_anchor_h192` is only n=3 and is **not** cited in the reply. `tsfm_earns_keep` (the 18/18) is n=3 × 6 datasets at H=192. `backbone_toggle_*` is n=3 × 6 datasets.
- **All win/loss counts in the reply are raw mean or per-seed comparisons; no significance test appears anywhere in the reply.** The result JSONs contain only `ria_beats_*` booleans (`<=` on raw MSE). I computed the paired t-tests above; they are not in any archived file.

I read all three documents and checked every load-bearing claim against the paper (and, where the reply cites rebuttal-only runs, against the repo's result files).

---

# Official Comment by Reviewer Pm4m — on the authors' second reply

I asked two questions. One is answered but the answer does not hold together; one is genuinely met, and then over-claimed in the final paragraph. Details below.

## (a) Which claim is correct

The authors commit to a side — §4.1 is right, the W3 clause was the error — and they supply a measurement rather than an argument. I credit both. But the paragraph carrying the answer contradicts itself.

> "Per-instance scaling subtracts each window's mean and divides by its scale, so the encoder never sees the location-scale"

> "The statistics are present in what the router reads, which is §4.1's claim."

Both cannot be true of the same tensor unless something reintroduces (M,Σ) between the scaler and the layer the probe reads. The reply never says what. If Moirai passes loc/scale through a side path, if the probe reads a tensor upstream of the scaler, if the level leaks through boundary effects — say which, because the whole settlement of (a) rests on it. As written, a claim the authors could not defend has been replaced by a pair of claims that cannot both stand, and I am asked to accept the second.

R²=0.996 versus −0.311 is also not symmetric evidence. A linear probe recovering μ at 0.996 proves presence. The same probe returning −0.311 on an eight-block encoder proves only that μ is not *linearly* recoverable — which is what one expects of a deep nonlinear encoder whether or not μ survives. ## Verdicts

**CLAIM 1 — PARTIAL (rebuttal sentence refuted; paper's Prop. 1 survives; allegation's wording is wrong)**
**CLAIM 2 — VERIFIED on substance (one factual error in the allegation, which makes the finding *worse*)**
**CLAIM 3 — VERIFIED, and understated**

---

# CLAIM 1 — Appendix H vs the conjunctive collapse rule

**The rule under test** (`/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/rebuttal/reply_pm4m_round2.md:13`):
> "both give the same verdict on every App. H case: collapse needs the statistics removed from what the router reads **and** a learnable affine map that can co-adapt (Prop. 1)."

### The table row (verified verbatim)
`/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/main.tex:1972` (table `tab:vision_moe`, App. H — `\appendix` at :1135, App. H = `\section{Normalization Generalization}`):
```latex
\multirow{2}{*}{ViT-B/16} & E & Frozen + InstanceNorm1d   & $\mathbf{0.000 \pm 0.000}$ & \textbf{Yes} & $0.953$ \\
```
Raw data confirms it exactly: `results/vision_moe_vit/vit_collapse_summary_{42,43,44}.json`, `E_frozen_instancenorm` test_entropy = 0.0000/0.0000/0.0000, acc 0.9537/0.9525/0.9519 (mean 0.9527 → "0.953").

### The code (`/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/scripts/run_vision_moe_vit_collapse.py`)
- **Normalizer, no affine** — line 168: `self.norm = nn.InstanceNorm1d(d_model, affine=False)`
- **Backbone frozen** — lines 285-289: `backbone.eval(); for p in backbone.parameters(): p.requires_grad = False; params = list(moe.parameters())`
- **What the router reads** — lines 222-224:
```python
router_feat = normed[:, 0]   # (B, D) — CLS token
gate_logits = self.router_gate(router_feat)
weights = F.softmax(gate_logits, dim=-1)
```

**The allegation's "no learnable affine map" is imprecise.** There *is* a trainable affine map between the normalizer and the gate logits: `self.router_gate = nn.Linear(d_model, K)` (line 187), plus five trainable experts that also read `normed` (lines 190-196, 227-228). What is absent is a trainable map *upstream* of the router's input — i.e. Prop. 1's `A`. That is the reading that matters, and under it case E has conjunct 1 only.

**It is a genuine dynamic collapse, not an init artifact.** From `trajectory_E_frozen_instancenorm_*.jsonl` (11,730 steps, `log K = 1.609`): step0 = 1.5898/1.4798/1.5549 → step20 ≈ 0.38/0.42/0.80 → final = 0.0000 on all three seeds. The backbone was frozen throughout.

### Case C (ResNet, unfrozen + no norm)
Paper: `main.tex:1969`, `0.184 ± 0.260`, collapse **Yes**. Source is `results/vision_moe_v2/run_42.log` + `run_multi.log`: final entropies **0.0747 / 0.0030 / 0.4737** (mean 0.1838; std ddof=1 = **0.2536**, not 0.260 — small numeric discrepancy). `norm_type = "none"` → **nothing stripped, yet collapse.** So case C has conjunct 2 only.

### Verdict on the rule
The rebuttal states two **necessary** conditions. Appendix H contains a counterexample to each:

| Case | statistics stripped from router input? | trainable `A` upstream? | collapses? |
|---|---|---|---|
| E (ViT) | yes | **no** (frozen) | **yes** |
| C (ResNet) | **no** | yes | **yes** |

Either conjunct alone suffices. The conjunction is falsified twice by the paper's own appendix. Under the alternative reading where "learnable affine map" means the router head `w`, the second conjunct is vacuous (every MoE has one) and the rule collapses to conjunct 1 — which case C then refutes.

### The strongest available defence — and it holds, for the paper only
Prop. 1's proof **explicitly anticipates case E**. `main.tex:1436-1437` (Part ii):
> "Note that this argument removes the co-adaptation mechanism but does not by itself preclude collapse from $\mathbf{w}$-only dynamics: if expert 1 were uniformly better than expert 2 across all inputs, $\dot{\mathbf{w}}$ would still drive $p \to 1$. Empirical non-collapse therefore **additionally requires** that $(\ell_1 - \ell_2)$ flips sign across input regimes, i.e. that experts specialize to different windows."

Prop. 1 licenses **two independent routes** to collapse: (a) `A`-mediated co-adaptation (case C), (b) `w`-only runaway when the router's input cannot support specialization — which is precisely what stripping causes (case E). The paper is internally consistent. **The rebuttal's shorthand is not** — it converted a disjunction into a conjunction.

**Fix that loses nothing:** state it disjunctively ("collapse follows either route: the statistics the router reads are stripped, so no specialization is possible even under a frozen backbone; or the backbone is trainable and co-adapts with the dominant expert"). This still gives the correct verdict on Moirai (neither route), so the rebuttal's conclusion survives the correction.

### Two further Appendix-H exposures created by "every App. H case"
1. **Table `tab:vision_moe` reports only 2 of the 6 ViT conditions that were run.** The omitted condition **G** is the RR-MoA analog (frozen + InstanceNorm1d + **raw-image routing**, `run_vision_moe_vit_collapse.py:403-407`) and it **collapses on 2 of 3 seeds**: test_entropy 0.0009 (s42), 0.0016 (s43), 0.9438 (s44) → 0.315 ± 0.544. Also omitted: J (frozen + LayerNorm) collapses 2/3 (0.0094, 0.6548, 0.0097); H (unfrozen + IN1d) 0.111 ± 0.157. Inviting a reviewer to check "every App. H case" points at the paper's own intervention failing in the vision control.
2. **The table mixes two metrics.** ResNet rows A–D use `entropy_final` = last *training-step* entropy (`run_vision_moe_collapse_v2.py:413,426`) with ddof=1 std; ViT rows E–F use `test_entropy` = mean over test batches (`run_vision_moe_vit_collapse.py:384,499`) with ddof=0 std (F: 0.494 ± 0.1293 ddof0 matches the paper's ±0.130; ddof1 would be 0.158). Separately, an earlier run of case C (`results/vision_moe/collapse_summary_{42,43}.json`) reports 1.5868 / 1.5946, `collapsed=False`.

---

# CLAIM 2 — Moirai's per-instance scaling in our path

### Traced path (used by both `stat_decodability_core.py` and the Moirai adapter runs)
`stat_decodability_core.py:85` → `_extract_features_batch` → `finetune.py:124` → `_forward_moirai`.

`/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/feasibility/finetune.py:167-199`:
```python
patches = x[:, :n_patches * patch_size].reshape(x.shape[0], n_patches, patch_size)
...
projected = model.in_proj(patches_padded, in_feat_size)   # line 193
...
encoder(projected)                                        # line 199
```
Raw patches → `in_proj` → `encoder`. **No scaler, no normalization of any kind.**

`/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/feasibility/model.py:90-93`: `load_moirai` returns `MoiraiModule.from_pretrained(model_name)`. Confirmed.

### The allegation's one factual error
**PackedStdScaler does NOT live in `MoiraiForecast`.** I downloaded the uni2ts sdists (not installed locally) and checked both versions — identical:

`uni2ts/model/moirai/module.py` (v2.0.0 :121, :181-186; v1.2.0 :101, :161-170):
```python
self.scaler = PackedStdScaler() if scaling else PackedNOPScaler()   # inside MoiraiModule.__init__
...
loc, scale = self.scaler(target, observed_mask * ~prediction_mask.unsqueeze(-1), sample_id, variate_id)
scaled_target = (target - loc) / scale
reprs = self.in_proj(scaled_target, patch_size)
reprs = self.encoder(masked_reprs, packed_attention_mask(sample_id), time_id=..., var_id=...)
```
Same for Moirai-MoE (`uni2ts/model/moirai_moe/module.py:121,190,196,198`).

**This makes the finding stronger.** The scaler is an attribute of the exact object we load; we bypass it by calling `model.in_proj` and `model.encoder` directly instead of `model(...)`. (We also skip `packed_attention_mask`, `time_id`, `var_id`, and `mask_encoding` — the forward is non-standard in more ways than the scaler.)

### MOMENT contrast — RevIN *is* applied
`finetune.py:130`: `model(x_enc=batch_x, input_mask=input_mask)` invokes `MOMENTPipeline.forward`, which runs `model.normalizer`. Direct empirical proof: swapping `model.normalizer` for identity (`model.py:28-33`, `disable_revin`) moves R²(μ) from **−0.3111 → 0.9994**. The −0.311 is real and comes from RevIN.

### Measured decodability (`results/stat_decodability/`)
| backbone | R²(μ) | R²(log σ) |
|---|---|---|
| Moirai (scaler bypassed) | **0.9960** | 0.9614 |
| MOMENT (RevIN active) | **−0.3111** | 0.6001 |
| MOMENT, RevIN off | 0.9994 | 0.9506 |
| Moirai-MoE | −0.0313 | −0.0000 |

⚠️ **Do not cite the Moirai-MoE row.** `results/stat_decodability_v2/moirai_moe_ETTh1.json` reports `feat_std_mean = 0.0`, `feat_eff_rank = 0` — the hidden states are identically constant. Its R² is a degenerate-feature artifact, not evidence about stripping.

### Answer to the framed question
**No.** §4.1 (`main.tex:410`) — "(ii) Moirai and Moirai-MoE, which use RMSNorm internally with only non-learnable per-instance I/O scaling … non-learnable I/O scaling **preserves** the (M,Σ) statistics in the hidden states the router reads" — does **not** accurately describe what our code does. Moirai's per-instance scaling is never executed in our path. The *empirical* claim (R²=0.996, statistics present) is correct; the *mechanistic attribution* is not. Under Moirai's own `forward`, `(target − loc)/scale` is applied before `in_proj`, structurally the same operation as RevIN. The honest framing is: "in our adapter path the encoder is driven directly through `in_proj`, so Moirai's I/O scaler is not in the loop and the (M,Σ) statistics survive into the hidden states the router reads (R²=0.996)."

The rebuttal's already-retracted clause ("Per-instance scaling subtracts each window's mean … so the encoder never sees the location-scale") correctly describes uni2ts, but not our runs — the retraction should say *why* (the scaler is bypassed), not just that the wording was loose.

---

# CLAIM 3 — Backbone toggle vs "the backbone earns its place on 5 of 6"

### The control is clean (allegation verified)
`/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/scripts/backbone_toggle_core.py`: one `_RECIPE` dict (lines 40-46) shared by both arms; `torch.manual_seed(seed); np.random.seed(seed)` re-set **before each arm** (lines 68-70); same splits, same scaler, same 30 epochs, same val early stopping. Only `backbone_off` differs (line 75).

Implementation, `scripts/run_gap_closing.py:404-405`: `if self.backbone_off: gates = torch.zeros_like(gates)`. Expert output is `base + gate * residual` (line 162), so the residual path is exactly zeroed. Sparse top-2 weights are `F.softmax(topk_vals)` (line 431) and sum to 1 over experts that all return the *same* shared `base` → the OFF arm's output is **exactly** the shared raw branch. The shared branch is `nn.Linear(input_len, output_dim)` (line 361) with the NLinear shift at line 156 (`base = self.raw_branch(raw_input - last) + last`), 49,248 params — architecturally identical to `_NLinearScratch` (`nlinear_anchor_core.py:48-59`).

### Full toggle data — 72 cells (4 horizons × 6 datasets × 3 seeds), % change from turning the backbone ON (negative = backbone helps)

| dataset | H=96 | H=192 | H=336 | H=720 | mean | helps | paired t (n=12) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | +1.82 | +6.34 | +5.17 | **+26.68** | **+10.00** | 0/12 | **p=0.017 (hurts)** |
| ETTh2 | +4.46 | −0.92 | +5.76 | +4.57 | +3.47 | 5/12 | p=0.149 ns |
| ETTm1 | +0.23 | −1.14 | +1.90 | +2.39 | +0.85 | 6/12 | p=0.290 ns |
| ETTm2 | +5.87 | +1.82 | +0.40 | +3.05 | +2.79 | 1/12 | **p=0.0032 (hurts)** |
| Weather | −3.08 | −3.89 | −3.21 | −4.40 | **−3.64** | **12/12** | **p<1e-6 (helps)** |
| Electricity | +2.69 | +2.04 | +3.16 | +2.86 | +2.69 | **0/12** | **p<1e-6 (hurts)** |
| **ALL** | +2.00 | +0.71 | +2.20 | +5.86 | **+2.69** | **24/72** | **pooled p=0.0043 (hurts)** |

(Worst individual cells: ETTh1 H720 s44 **+40.68%**, s42 +25.37%, ETTh2 H336 s44 +19.18%.)

**The backbone helps on 1 of 6 datasets, not 5.** Pooled over all 72 matched pairs, turning the backbone on makes MSE *significantly worse*.

### The two clauses of the rebuttal sentence
- **"earns its place on 5 of 6 datasets"** — refuted. Toggle supports **1 of 6** (Weather).
- **"and on 9 of 10 cells where anchoring adds nothing"** (= Weather + Electricity) — **half inverted**. Weather: backbone helps 12/12, −3.64%, p<1e-6 ✓. Electricity: backbone **hurts** 0/12, +2.69%, p<1e-6 ✗.

### Why the anchor comparison and the toggle disagree — the identification is false
`rebuttal/reply_pm4m_round2.md:25`: "Close the gate and what remains is this anchor. The two therefore differ only in the backbone path." Architecturally true; **as run, false**. `nlinear_anchor_core.py:64-73`: the from-scratch anchor is `Adam lr=1e-3, 15 epochs, batch 128`, no warmup, no cosine, no val early stopping, no grad clip. The gate-closed arm gets 30 epochs, `cosine_schedule=True`, `warmup_epochs=5`, `val_early_stop=True, val_patience=5`, `grad_clip=1.0`.

**Decomposition at H=96** (recipe effect = gate-closed vs from-scratch, *identical architecture*; backbone effect = matched on/off):

| dataset | recipe effect | backbone effect | total RIA+ vs NLinear |
|---|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | −1.25% | +1.81% | +2.17% |
| ETTh2 | −1.48% | +4.43% | +1.10% |
| ETTm1 | −1.29% | +0.22% | −2.00% |
| ETTm2 | −5.17% | **+5.87%** | −2.58% |
| Weather | −1.16% | **−3.08%** | −3.78% |
| **Electricity** | **−6.59%** | **+2.69%** | −4.01% |

On 5 of 6 datasets the entire margin over the from-scratch anchor is the **training protocol**; on 4 of those the backbone subtracts from it. Only Weather is backbone-driven. Seed-matched cross-check (seeds 42/43/44 present in both suites) shows the two suites' RIA+ arms agree to ~1–3%, so this is not a seed artifact.

### Secondary: the "5 of 6" figure itself does not reproduce
From `results/nlinear_anchor_h96` (n=10, all 60 files):

| dataset | vs NLinear (mean / median / seed-wins / p) | vs DLinear (mean / median / seed-wins / p) |
|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | +2.20% / +2.27% / 2-10 / **p=0.043 loss** | +2.41% / +2.46% / 2-10 / **p=0.020 loss** |
| ETTh2 | +1.29% / +1.97% / 4-10 / ns | −10.72% / −8.10% / 8-10 / p=0.036 |
| ETTm1 | −1.47% / +1.55% / 4-10 / ns | +0.82% / **+0.03%** / 5-10 / ns |
| ETTm2 | −2.18% / −0.42% / 7-10 / ns | −11.52% / −4.64% / 10-10 / p=0.052 |
| Weather | −3.74% / −3.79% / 10-10 / p=0.0025 | −3.74% / −3.65% / 9-10 / p=0.0024 |
| Electricity | −3.97% / −3.06% / 10-10 / p=0.0004 | −2.54% / −2.71% / 9-10 / p=0.0013 |

**4/6 by mean against each anchor (3/6 by median vs NLinear), not 5/6.** Also, "ETTm1 within 0.1% of NLinear" is wrong: ETTm1 vs NLinear is −1.47% mean / +1.55% median. The **+0.03%** figure belongs to **ETTm1 vs DLinear (median)**, i.e. the parenthetical attaches to the wrong anchor.

### What the toggle data would actually support saying
> A matched gate-closed control (identical recipe, seed, schedule and early stopping; 4 horizons × 6 datasets × 3 seeds, 72 paired runs) isolates the backbone path directly. The frozen backbone contributes a significant, uniform gain on Weather (−3.6%, 12/12 cells, p<1e-6) and is statistically neutral on ETTh2 and ETTm1; on ETTh1, ETTm2 and Electricity the gate-closed model matches or beats it, with ETTh1 degrading at long horizons (+26.7% at H=720). We therefore do not claim the backbone earns its place everywhere: on this recipe its value is dataset-dependent, and most of Residual-IA⁺'s margin over the from-scratch anchor comes from the training protocol rather than the backbone path — which is consistent with R(D) and with why we ship the raw branch as the primary predictor.

---

## Caveats
- Toggle uses n=3 seeds vs the anchor suite's n=10; seed-matched cross-check (above) rules out a seed artifact.
- `uni2ts` is unpinned on Modal (`scripts/modal_stat_decodability.py:34`, `.pip_install("uni2ts")`); I verified the scaler placement in **both** 1.2.0 and 2.0.0 — identical in both, so the conclusion is version-robust.
- `uni2ts` is not installed locally, so the Moirai path finding is from source reading, not execution. It is unambiguous: `_forward_moirai` never calls `model(...)`.

| Case | statistics stripped from router input? | trainable `A` upstream? | collapses? |
|---|---|---|---|
| E (ViT) | yes | **no** (frozen) | **yes** |
| C (ResNet) | **no** | yes | **yes** |

Either conjunct alone suffices. The conjunction is falsified twice by the paper's own appendix. Under the alternative reading where "learnable affine map" means the router head `w`, the second conjunct is vacuous (every MoE has one) and the rule collapses to conjunct 1 — which case C then refutes.

### The strongest available defence — and it holds, for the paper only
Prop. 1's proof **explicitly anticipates case E**. `main.tex:1436-1437` (Part ii):
> "Note that this argument removes the co-adaptation mechanism but does not by itself preclude collapse from $\mathbf{w}$-only dynamics: if expert 1 were uniformly better than expert 2 across all inputs, $\dot{\mathbf{w}}$ would still drive $p \to 1$. Empirical non-collapse therefore **additionally requires** that $(\ell_1 - \ell_2)$ flips sign across input regimes, i.e. that experts specialize to different windows."

Prop. 1 licenses **two independent routes** to collapse: (a) `A`-mediated co-adaptation (case C), (b) `w`-only runaway when the router's input cannot support specialization — which is precisely what stripping causes (case E). The paper is internally consistent. **The rebuttal's shorthand is not** — it converted a disjunction into a conjunction.

**Fix that loses nothing:** state it disjunctively ("collapse follows either route: the statistics the router reads are stripped, so no specialization is possible even under a frozen backbone; or the backbone is trainable and co-adapts with the dominant expert"). This still gives the correct verdict on Moirai (neither route), so the rebuttal's conclusion survives the correction.

### Two further Appendix-H exposures created by "every App. H case"
1. **Table `tab:vision_moe` reports only 2 of the 6 ViT conditions that were run.** The omitted condition **G** is the RR-MoA analog (frozen + InstanceNorm1d + **raw-image routing**, `run_vision_moe_vit_collapse.py:403-407`) and it **collapses on 2 of 3 seeds**: test_entropy 0.0009 (s42), 0.0016 (s43), 0.9438 (s44) → 0.315 ± 0.544. Also omitted: J (frozen + LayerNorm) collapses 2/3 (0.0094, 0.6548, 0.0097); H (unfrozen + IN1d) 0.111 ± 0.157. Inviting a reviewer to check "every App. H case" points at the paper's own intervention failing in the vision control.
2. **The table mixes two metrics.** ResNet rows A–D use `entropy_final` = last *training-step* entropy (`run_vision_moe_collapse_v2.py:413,426`) with ddof=1 std; ViT rows E–F use `test_entropy` = mean over test batches (`run_vision_moe_vit_collapse.py:384,499`) with ddof=0 std (F: 0.494 ± 0.1293 ddof0 matches the paper's ±0.130; ddof1 would be 0.158). Separately, an earlier run of case C (`results/vision_moe/collapse_summary_{42,43}.json`) reports 1.5868 / 1.5946, `collapsed=False`.

---

# CLAIM 2 — Moirai's per-instance scaling in our path

### Traced path (used by both `stat_decodability_core.py` and the Moirai adapter runs)
`stat_decodability_core.py:85` → `_extract_features_batch` → `finetune.py:124` → `_forward_moirai`.

`/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/feasibility/finetune.py:167-199`:
```python
patches = x[:, :n_patches * patch_size].reshape(x.shape[0], n_patches, patch_size)
...
projected = model.in_proj(patches_padded, in_feat_size)   # line 193
...
encoder(projected)                                        # line 199
```
Raw patches → `in_proj` → `encoder`. **No scaler, no normalization of any kind.**

`/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/feasibility/model.py:90-93`: `load_moirai` returns `MoiraiModule.from_pretrained(model_name)`. Confirmed.

### The allegation's one factual error
**PackedStdScaler does NOT live in `MoiraiForecast`.** I downloaded the uni2ts sdists (not installed locally) and checked both versions — identical:

`uni2ts/model/moirai/module.py` (v2.0.0 :121, :181-186; v1.2.0 :101, :161-170):
```python
self.scaler = PackedStdScaler() if scaling else PackedNOPScaler()   # inside MoiraiModule.__init__
...
loc, scale = self.scaler(target, observed_mask * ~prediction_mask.unsqueeze(-1), sample_id, variate_id)
scaled_target = (target - loc) / scale
reprs = self.in_proj(scaled_target, patch_size)
reprs = self.encoder(masked_reprs, packed_attention_mask(sample_id), time_id=..., var_id=...)
```
Same for Moirai-MoE (`uni2ts/model/moirai_moe/module.py:121,190,196,198`).

**This makes the finding stronger.** The scaler is an attribute of the exact object we load; we bypass it by calling `model.in_proj` and `model.encoder` directly instead of `model(...)`. (We also skip `packed_attention_mask`, `time_id`, `var_id`, and `mask_encoding` — the forward is non-standard in more ways than the scaler.)

### MOMENT contrast — RevIN *is* applied
`finetune.py:130`: `model(x_enc=batch_x, input_mask=input_mask)` invokes `MOMENTPipeline.forward`, which runs `model.normalizer`. Direct empirical proof: swapping `model.normalizer` for identity (`model.py:28-33`, `disable_revin`) moves R²(μ) from **−0.3111 → 0.9994**. The −0.311 is real and comes from RevIN.

### Measured decodability (`results/stat_decodability/`)
| backbone | R²(μ) | R²(log σ) |
|---|---|---|
| Moirai (scaler bypassed) | **0.9960** | 0.9614 |
| MOMENT (RevIN active) | **−0.3111** | 0.6001 |
| MOMENT, RevIN off | 0.9994 | 0.9506 |
| Moirai-MoE | −0.0313 | −0.0000 |

⚠️ **Do not cite the Moirai-MoE row.** `results/stat_decodability_v2/moirai_moe_ETTh1.json` reports `feat_std_mean = 0.0`, `feat_eff_rank = 0` — the hidden states are identically constant. Its R² is a degenerate-feature artifact, not evidence about stripping.

### Answer to the framed question
**No.** §4.1 (`main.tex:410`) — "(ii) Moirai and Moirai-MoE, which use RMSNorm internally with only non-learnable per-instance I/O scaling … non-learnable I/O scaling **preserves** the (M,Σ) statistics in the hidden states the router reads" — does **not** accurately describe what our code does. Moirai's per-instance scaling is never executed in our path. The *empirical* claim (R²=0.996, statistics present) is correct; the *mechanistic attribution* is not. Under Moirai's own `forward`, `(target − loc)/scale` is applied before `in_proj`, structurally the same operation as RevIN. The honest framing is: "in our adapter path the encoder is driven directly through `in_proj`, so Moirai's I/O scaler is not in the loop and the (M,Σ) statistics survive into the hidden states the router reads (R²=0.996)."

The rebuttal's already-retracted clause ("Per-instance scaling subtracts each window's mean … so the encoder never sees the location-scale") correctly describes uni2ts, but not our runs — the retraction should say *why* (the scaler is bypassed), not just that the wording was loose.

---

# CLAIM 3 — Backbone toggle vs "the backbone earns its place on 5 of 6"

### The control is clean (allegation verified)
`/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/scripts/backbone_toggle_core.py`: one `_RECIPE` dict (lines 40-46) shared by both arms; `torch.manual_seed(seed); np.random.seed(seed)` re-set **before each arm** (lines 68-70); same splits, same scaler, same 30 epochs, same val early stopping. Only `backbone_off` differs (line 75).

Implementation, `scripts/run_gap_closing.py:404-405`: `if self.backbone_off: gates = torch.zeros_like(gates)`. Expert output is `base + gate * residual` (line 162), so the residual path is exactly zeroed. Sparse top-2 weights are `F.softmax(topk_vals)` (line 431) and sum to 1 over experts that all return the *same* shared `base` → the OFF arm's output is **exactly** the shared raw branch. The shared branch is `nn.Linear(input_len, output_dim)` (line 361) with the NLinear shift at line 156 (`base = self.raw_branch(raw_input - last) + last`), 49,248 params — architecturally identical to `_NLinearScratch` (`nlinear_anchor_core.py:48-59`).

### Full toggle data — 72 cells (4 horizons × 6 datasets × 3 seeds), % change from turning the backbone ON (negative = backbone helps)

| dataset | H=96 | H=192 | H=336 | H=720 | mean | helps | paired t (n=12) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | +1.82 | +6.34 | +5.17 | **+26.68** | **+10.00** | 0/12 | **p=0.017 (hurts)** |
| ETTh2 | +4.46 | −0.92 | +5.76 | +4.57 | +3.47 | 5/12 | p=0.149 ns |
| ETTm1 | +0.23 | −1.14 | +1.90 | +2.39 | +0.85 | 6/12 | p=0.290 ns |
| ETTm2 | +5.87 | +1.82 | +0.40 | +3.05 | +2.79 | 1/12 | **p=0.0032 (hurts)** |
| Weather | −3.08 | −3.89 | −3.21 | −4.40 | **−3.64** | **12/12** | **p<1e-6 (helps)** |
| Electricity | +2.69 | +2.04 | +3.16 | +2.86 | +2.69 | **0/12** | **p<1e-6 (hurts)** |
| **ALL** | +2.00 | +0.71 | +2.20 | +5.86 | **+2.69** | **24/72** | **pooled p=0.0043 (hurts)** |

(Worst individual cells: ETTh1 H720 s44 **+40.68%**, s42 +25.37%, ETTh2 H336 s44 +19.18%.)

**The backbone helps on 1 of 6 datasets, not 5.** Pooled over all 72 matched pairs, turning the backbone on makes MSE *significantly worse*.

### The two clauses of the rebuttal sentence
- **"earns its place on 5 of 6 datasets"** — refuted. Toggle supports **1 of 6** (Weather).
- **"and on 9 of 10 cells where anchoring adds nothing"** (= Weather + Electricity) — **half inverted**. Weather: backbone helps 12/12, −3.64%, p<1e-6 ✓. Electricity: backbone **hurts** 0/12, +2.69%, p<1e-6 ✗.

### Why the anchor comparison and the toggle disagree — the identification is false
`rebuttal/reply_pm4m_round2.md:25`: "Close the gate and what remains is this anchor. The two therefore differ only in the backbone path." Architecturally true; **as run, false**. `nlinear_anchor_core.py:64-73`: the from-scratch anchor is `Adam lr=1e-3, 15 epochs, batch 128`, no warmup, no cosine, no val early stopping, no grad clip. The gate-closed arm gets 30 epochs, `cosine_schedule=True`, `warmup_epochs=5`, `val_early_stop=True, val_patience=5`, `grad_clip=1.0`.

**Decomposition at H=96** (recipe effect = gate-closed vs from-scratch, *identical architecture*; backbone effect = matched on/off):

| dataset | recipe effect | backbone effect | total RIA+ vs NLinear |
|---|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | −1.25% | +1.81% | +2.17% |
| ETTh2 | −1.48% | +4.43% | +1.10% |
| ETTm1 | −1.29% | +0.22% | −2.00% |
| ETTm2 | −5.17% | **+5.87%** | −2.58% |
| Weather | −1.16% | **−3.08%** | −3.78% |
| **Electricity** | **−6.59%** | **+2.69%** | −4.01% |

On 5 of 6 datasets the entire margin over the from-scratch anchor is the **training protocol**; on 4 of those the backbone subtracts from it. Only Weather is backbone-driven. Seed-matched cross-check (seeds 42/43/44 present in both suites) shows the two suites' RIA+ arms agree to ~1–3%, so this is not a seed artifact.

### Secondary: the "5 of 6" figure itself does not reproduce
From `results/nlinear_anchor_h96` (n=10, all 60 files):

| dataset | vs NLinear (mean / median / seed-wins / p) | vs DLinear (mean / median / seed-wins / p) |
|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | +2.20% / +2.27% / 2-10 / **p=0.043 loss** | +2.41% / +2.46% / 2-10 / **p=0.020 loss** |
| ETTh2 | +1.29% / +1.97% / 4-10 / ns | −10.72% / −8.10% / 8-10 / p=0.036 |
| ETTm1 | −1.47% / +1.55% / 4-10 / ns | +0.82% / **+0.03%** / 5-10 / ns |
| ETTm2 | −2.18% / −0.42% / 7-10 / ns | −11.52% / −4.64% / 10-10 / p=0.052 |
| Weather | −3.74% / −3.79% / 10-10 / p=0.0025 | −3.74% / −3.65% / 9-10 / p=0.0024 |
| Electricity | −3.97% / −3.06% / 10-10 / p=0.0004 | −2.54% / −2.71% / 9-10 / p=0.0013 |

**4/6 by mean against each anchor (3/6 by median vs NLinear), not 5/6.** Also, "ETTm1 within 0.1% of NLinear" is wrong: ETTm1 vs NLinear is −1.47% mean / +1.55% median. The **+0.03%** figure belongs to **ETTm1 vs DLinear (median)**, i.e. the parenthetical attaches to the wrong anchor.

### What the toggle data would actually support saying
> A matched gate-closed control (identical recipe, seed, schedule and early stopping; 4 horizons × 6 datasets × 3 seeds, 72 paired runs) isolates the backbone path directly. The frozen backbone contributes a significant, uniform gain on Weather (−3.6%, 12/12 cells, p<1e-6) and is statistically neutral on ETTh2 and ETTm1; on ETTh1, ETTm2 and Electricity the gate-closed model matches or beats it, with ETTh1 degrading at long horizons (+26.7% at H=720). We therefore do not claim the backbone earns its place everywhere: on this recipe its value is dataset-dependent, and most of Residual-IA⁺'s margin over the from-scratch anchor comes from the training protocol rather than the backbone path — which is consistent with R(D) and with why we ship the raw branch as the primary predictor.

## Caveats
- Toggle uses n=3 seeds vs the anchor suite's n=10; seed-matched cross-check (above) rules out a seed artifact.
- `uni2ts` is unpinned on Modal (`scripts/modal_stat_decodability.py:34`, `.pip_install("uni2ts")`); I verified the scaler placement in **both** 1.2.0 and 2.0.0 — identical in both, so the conclusion is version-robust.
- `uni2ts` is not installed locally, so the Moirai path finding is from source reading, not execution. It is unambiguous: `_forward_moirai` never calls `model(...)`.

aiTitle: Prepare rebuttal response to reviewer PM4M's round 2 comments

content.text:
## (a) Is the Moirai-MoE feature extraction broken? **YES — confirmed, with an exact mechanism**

The features fed to the router/experts for `moirai_moe` are **identically zero at the encoder input**, and therefore constant at the encoder output.

**The chain:**

1. `/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/feasibility/standard_data.py:147-148` — `_detect_backbone_type("Salesforce/moirai-moe-1.0-R-small")` returns `"moirai"`. There is **no moirai-moe branch**:
   ```python
   if "moirai" in name:
       return "moirai"
   ```
2. `/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/feasibility/finetune.py:124` dispatches to `_forward_moirai`.
3. `/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/feasibility/finetune.py:180` — **`patch_size = 32` is hardcoded**.
4. `/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/feasibility/finetune.py:189-193`:
   ```python
   max_feat = max(model.patch_sizes)
   patches_padded = torch.nn.functional.pad(patches, (0, max_feat - patch_size))
   in_feat_size = torch.full(patches.shape[:2], patch_size, dtype=torch.long, device=patches.device)
   projected = model.in_proj(patches_padded, in_feat_size)
   ```
5. **Moirai-MoE's `patch_sizes` is `[16]`** — verified against the authoritative HF config (`https://huggingface.co/Salesforce/moirai-moe-1.0-R-small/raw/main/config.json` → `"patch_sizes": [16]`). Moirai-1.1-R-small is `[8, 16, 32, 64, 128]`.
   - `max_feat - patch_size = 16 - 32 = -16` → `F.pad` with a **negative** pad **truncates**, silently discarding the second half of every 32-sample patch (a separate, second bug).
   - `in_feat_size = 32` is passed to `MultiInSizeLinear(in_features_ls=(16,), ...)`.
6. `MultiInSizeLinear.forward` (uni2ts `uni2ts/module/ts_embed.py:89-102`, **identical in 1.2.0 and 2.0.0**):
   ```python
   out = 0
   for idx, feat_size in enumerate(self.in_features_ls):   # only 16
       out = out + (torch.eq(in_feat_size, feat_size).unsqueeze(-1)
                    * (einsum(weight, x, "out inp, ... inp -> ... out") + bias))
   return out
   ```
   `in_feat_size=32` matches **nothing** → every term is gated by `False` → **`in_proj` returns exactly zero for every token of every sample**. No exception is raised.
7. `/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/feasibility/finetune.py:199` `encoder(projected)` runs zeros through 6 layers; the hooked last-block output is constant across all inputs.

Empirical corroboration: `results/stat_decodability_v2/moirai_moe_ETTh1.json` has `feat_std_mean = 0.0`, `feat_eff_rank = 0`. Per `scripts/stat_decodability_core.py:126-127`, `eff_rank == 0` requires the centered feature matrix to be **exactly** zero.

Note `/Users/hungpq2412/neuralips26/feasibility/model.py:112-115` documents `patch_sizes = [16]` and then asserts *"The feature-extraction path handles this automatically via the model's own in_proj module"* — that assertion is false.

## (b) Does it contaminate the paper's Moirai-MoE results? **YES — confirmed**

**Same code path, verified:** `scripts/run_moirai_moe_vm.sh` is the driver for the 60-run table. It calls `scripts/run_rr_moa.py` and `scripts/run_adamix.py` with `--backbone Salesforce/moirai-moe-1.0-R-small`. Both do `bb_type = _detect_backbone_type(args.backbone)` (`run_adamix.py:630`, `run_rr_moa.py:613` → `"moirai"`) and then `_extract_features_batch(..., backbone_type=bb_type)` at `run_adamix.py:415,485` / `run_rr_moa.py:451,487`. The fixed-adapter baselines go through `feasibility/standard_data.py:190,206`, same function. `submission/feasibility/finetune.py` is **byte-identical** to the working tree here, so this is the code that produced the submitted numbers.

**Three independent behavioural fingerprints:**

1. **Three architecturally unrelated fixed adapters agree to 4 decimals.** `results/rr_moa/ETTh1_H96_K5_top2_frozen_42_bb-moirai-moe.json`: linear `1.154621`, attention `1.154710`, conv `1.154226` (36,960 / 37,345 / **192,864** params). Across all 30 Moirai-MoE frozen cells the max−min baseline spread is **median 0.28%** (min 0.004%, max 1.04%). Same measurement on plain Moirai: **median 19.4%** (1.0–59.0%); MOMENT-small ETTh1: **median 17.2%**. Adapter architecture cannot matter when the input is constant.

2. **AdaMix entropy is exactly log 5 in 30/30 cells** (1.6094226–1.6094376; log 5 = 1.6094379), routing weights 0.198–0.201. This is the *necessary* output of a hidden-state router (`run_adamix.py` `router_input="hidden"` default → `self.router(hidden_states.mean(dim=1))`) whose input is constant. The Table N.2 caption at `main.tex:2216` explains it as load-balance saturation "**even when the hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse**" — that clause is directly falsified by `feat_std_mean = 0.0`. The paper's own diagnostic only flags entropy → 0 as collapse, so a dead-constant router input is scored as "healthy."

3. **The −37% to −90% RR-MoA wins are what the degenerate configuration predicts.** RR-MoA experts **do** consume hidden states — `run_rr_moa.py:340` `outputs = torch.stack([a(hidden_states) for a in self.adapters], dim=1)` and `:355` `self.adapters[k](hidden_states[mask])` (class docstring: "the adapters see the backbone's hidden states"). With h constant, each expert emits a fixed vector c_k and the prediction reduces to Σ_k w_k(x_raw)·c_k — a 5-prototype blend steered **entirely by the conv router on the raw window**. The fixed baselines have no raw path, so they degenerate to a single constant (best case: mean of Y), giving MSE ≈ 1.15 / 3.06 / 1.12 / 3.11 / 0.61 / 1.06 — exactly the "AdaMix MSE" column. model_name: str = "Salesforce/moirai-moe-1.0-R-small") -> nn.Module:
    """Load Moirai-MoE (native mixture-of-experts TSFM).

    Moirai-MoE shares the same external interface as Moirai
    (`.in_proj`, `.patch_sizes`, `.encoder` with `.layers`, `.d_model`),
    so the existing `_forward_moirai` / `_get_encoder_blocks` /
    `_get_hidden_dim` helpers handle it without modification.  The only
    difference is the pre-trained weights contain internal expert routing
    inside each encoder block's FFN.  This lets us evaluate whether RR-MoA
    adapter-level routing is still beneficial on a backbone that already
    contains experts (B2 of the NeurIPS push plan).

    Note: Moirai-MoE d_model = 384 (same as Moirai-1.1-R-small), and
    patch_sizes = [16] (vs [16, 32, 64, 128] for regular Moirai-1.1).  The
    feature-extraction path handles this automatically via the model's own
    in_proj module.
    """
    from uni2ts.model.moirai_moe import MoiraiMoEModule
    model = MoiraiMoEModule.from_pretrained(model_name)
    model = model.to(device)
    model.eval()
    return model

python3 - <<'EOF'
import json,glob,statistics as st
from collections import defaultdict
for d in ['nlinear_anchor_mmlarge_h96','nlinear_anchor_moirai_h96','nlinear_anchor_h192','nlinear_anchor_mmlarge_papercfg','nlinear_anchor_exchange']:
    fs=[p for p in sorted(glob.glob(f'results/{d}/*_s*.json'))]
    if not fs: continue
    by=defaultdict(list)
    for p in fs:
        j=json.load(open(p)); by[j['dataset']].append(j)
    print(f"\n=== {d} ({len(fs)} runs) ===")
    wdl=wnl=wbest=0; n=0
    for ds,rows in sorted(by.items()):
        ria=st.mean([r['ria_mse'] for r in rows]); dl=st.mean([r['dlinear_mse'] for r in rows]); nl=st.mean([r['nlinear_mse'] for r in rows])
        vdl=(ria-dl)/dl*100; vnl=(ria-nl)/nl*100; best=min(dl,nl); vb=(ria-best)/best*100
        n+=1; wdl+= vdl<=0; wnl+= vnl<=0; wbest+= vb<=0
        print(f"  {ds:12} n={len(rows)} RIA={ria:.4f} DL={dl:.4f} NL={nl:.4f}  vsDL={vdl:+6.2f}% vsNL={vnl:+6.2f}% vsBEST={vb:+6.2f}%")
    print(f"  --> vs DLinear {wdl}/{n} | vs NLinear {wnl}/{n} | vs BEST-of-anchor {wbest}/{n}")
EOF
