aiTitle: Prepare rebuttal response to reviewer PM4M's round 2 comments

content.text:
I ran four verification agents and then re-derived every disputed number myself from the raw JSONs. **The reply is not ready to post.** One paragraph is refuted by our own data, one sentence invites the reviewer into a falsifying appendix, and there's a separate severe finding.

## Blocker 1 — the new final paragraph is contradicted by our own control

The uncommitted edit claims "the comparison above is also a backbone control: the backbone earns its place on 5 of 6 datasets, and on 9 of 10 cells where anchoring adds nothing."

We already ran the real control (`scripts/backbone_toggle_core.py` — same recipe, seed, schedule; only the gate zeroed). 72 matched pairs:

| H | backbone helps | pooled mean |
|---|---|---|
| 96 | 1/6 datasets (Weather) | +2.00% worse |
| 192 | 3/6 | +0.71% worse |
| 336 | 1/6 | +2.20% worse |
| 720 | 1/6 (ETTh1 +26.7%) | +5.86% worse |

Pooled: backbone helps **1 of 6 datasets**, mean **+2.69% worse**. Electricity — one of the two datasets the paragraph names — is 0/12. The identification is also false as run: RIA+ gets 30 epochs, cosine, 5-epoch warmup, val early-stop; the anchor gets 15 fixed epochs of plain Adam. Reverting to HEAD doesn't fix it either: HEAD calls this control "future work" for an experiment that is now finished.

## Blocker 2 — "both give the same verdict on every App. H case" is false, and points the reviewer at the proof

`main.tex:1972`, case E: ViT-B/16, **frozen** + `InstanceNorm1d(affine=False)` → entropy **0.000, collapse Yes**. No learnable affine, frozen backbone — the reply's conjunctive rule predicts *no* collapse. Case C (unfrozen, *no* norm) collapses at 0.184 with nothing stripped, killing the other conjunct. Fix is cheap and correct: state it disjunctively — Prop. 1's own proof (`main.tex:1436-1437`) already licenses w-only collapse, and the disjunctive form still gives "no collapse" for Moirai.

## Blocker 3 — section 1 contradicts itself, exactly as the reviewer will read it

"the encoder never sees the location-scale" vs "the mean is recoverable (R²=0.996)" cannot both hold. The actual reason: `feasibility/finetune.py:167-199` drives `model.in_proj` → `model.encoder` directly and never calls `model(...)`, so **no per-instance scaling runs in our path at all**. Either disclose that in a clause or delete the mechanism sentence — leaving it is the one thing guaranteed to lose the point.

## Also load-bearing

- **"5/6 against each anchor" is source-dependent.** Against the *paired in-run* anchors it's 4/6 and 4/6. The 5/6 needs the standalone anchor run plus counting ETTm1 (+0.10% vs NLinear) as a match and ETTh1 (−0.02%) as a win. **Best-of-anchor is 3/6** — and the reviewer's own "against the stronger anchor" phrasing for Solar invites computing it.
- **"We are extending the anchor to the other backbones" — already done, and unfavourable.** MOMENT-large 3/6, Moirai 3/6, H=192 3/6 vs best-of-anchor (`results/nlinear_anchor_{mmlarge,moirai}_h96`, `_h192`). Promising a pending extension you've already run reads badly if it ever surfaces.
- **Σ is free.** §4.1 claims (M,Σ); we report only M. R²(log σ): Moirai 0.961, MOMENT+RevIN 0.600, RevIN-off 0.951.
- **Table N.2 is Moirai-MoE; W3's gain is Moirai.** Quoting that caption as authority mismatches backbones, and the reviewer noticed in simulation.

## Separate and severe: the Moirai-MoE results are contaminated

`_forward_moirai` hardcodes `patch_size=32`, but Moirai-MoE's `patch_sizes=[16]` (our own `feasibility/model.py:113` says so). `MultiInSizeLinear` returns exactly zero when the size doesn't match, so the hidden states are constant — `feat_std_mean=0.0`, `eff_rank=0`. Fingerprints confirm it: three architecturally different adapters (37K/37K/193K params) agree to 0.04–0.33% on Moirai-MoE vs 3.6–8.9% spread on plain Moirai, and AdaMix entropy is exactly log 5 in 30/30 cells. Same path produced the paper's 60 Moirai-MoE runs (`run_moirai_moe_vm.sh` → `run_rr_moa.py:451`). Plain Moirai is fine.

This hits Table N.2, the main-text "37–90%" claim, and the round-1 rebuttal's "Moirai-MoE 15/15."

## What I'd do

Rewrite section 2's ending around the toggle we actually ran and report it whatever it says — the reviewer named that exact control as condition #1 for raising the score, and we've now made two claims about backbone attribution that our own data refutes. Conceding "the backbone's value is dataset-dependent on this recipe" costs less than a third retraction. Then fix the disjunctive rule, disclose the extraction path in one clause, add Σ, and lead with best-of-anchor.

Two calls are yours: (1) whether to disclose the backbone toggle result, which substantially concedes W4's "dead weight" charge; (2) what to do about Moirai-MoE before the discussion window closes. Say which way you want to go and I'll write the revision.

Yes to all three. Precisely:

## 1. The NLinear run went against us on part of the claim

It didn't refute the method; it shrank it, and it hit exactly the cells we led with.

| | vs DLinear | vs NLinear |
|---|---|---|
| ETTh2 | −12.5% | **+1.1%** (n.s.) |
| ETTm2 | −13.7% | **−2.6%** (n.s.) |
| Exchange | −26.3% | **+0.5%** (parity), behind at H=192 |
| Weather | −3.8% (p=.002) | −3.8% (p=.003) |
| Electricity | −2.6% (p=.001) | −4.0% (p=.0004) |
| ETTh1 | +2.4% loss | +2.2% loss |

Counts at H=96, MOMENT-small: 5/6 vs DLinear, 4/6 vs NLinear, **3/6 vs the better anchor per dataset**. Solar (20/20 vs the stronger anchor) and the two significant survivors are genuinely ours. The three biggest headline margins were mostly the level anchor. And the cross-backbone extension is already run and lands the same: 3/6 best-of-anchor on MOMENT-large, 3/6 on Moirai, 3/6 at H=192.

## 2. The reviewer is right, and their charge is weaker than the truth

Their literal point is correct: the 65:11 grid uses one anchor, and Residual-IA+'s own base predictor is the other Zeng variant, so the grid can't separate the two.

But beating NLinear wouldn't have proved "the backbone adds value" either, because Residual-IA+ vs a from-scratch anchor also differs in training protocol. The only thing that isolates the backbone is the gate. Decomposing at H=96 (seeds 42–44) with our own toggle:

| dataset | recipe effect | backbone effect | total vs NLinear |
|---|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | −2.64% | +1.81% | −0.87% |
| ETTh2 | −1.50% | +4.43% | +2.86% |
| ETTm1 | +0.87% | +0.22% | +1.10% |
| ETTm2 | −1.73% | +5.87% | +4.03% |
| Electricity | **−6.21%** | +2.69% | −3.69% |
| Weather | −1.63% | **−3.08%** | −4.66% |

On five of six datasets the training recipe is what beats the anchor and the backbone *subtracts* from it. Weather is the only place the backbone earns its keep. So the reviewer suspected a confound; the direct control says the backbone contributes negatively on average.

## 3. The round-1 "18/18 / decisive at H≥192" claim is wrong twice

The number is real — `results/tsfm_earns_keep`, 18/18, mean −11.79%. What's wrong:

- **The description.** "Holding the raw branch fixed and toggling only the backbone" is not what ran. The comparator is the Raw-MLP MoE, which replaces the raw branch with K=5 two-layer MLPs (`main.tex:2840`). Both arms changed.
- **The conclusion.** The matched toggle at that same horizon says backbone helps 3/6 datasets, pooled +0.71% worse. At H=336 it's 1/6 (+2.20%), at H=720 1/6 (+5.86%, ETTh1 +26.7%). "At H≥192 it is decisive" is the reverse of what our own control shows.

So round 1 asserted an architectural argument as a control, and the working-tree paragraph in round 2 does the same thing again in the other direction. That pattern is what a reviewer counting retractions will price in.

The one genuinely strong move left is to report the toggle ourselves, plainly, and re-scope the contribution to the diagnosis + R(D) + raw-vs-hidden routing, which the toggle doesn't touch. Want me to draft that version?

content.text:
Not all of it. Three of the five claims hold; the horizon thesis is the part that fails, and it's stated twice.

## Holds up

- **"546-run sweep, one-time, not per-dataset."** `main.tex:2555` confirms the sweep. The framing is yours and it stands.
- **"Generalizes to unseen data without re-tuning" (8 of 9 cells).** Verified in `results/ria_offsuite` (Solar 3/3 −9.55%, Traffic 3/3 −1.53%, Exchange 2/3 −23.75%), and it *survives* the stronger anchor at n=10: Solar −8.7%, Traffic −2.3% vs NLinear, Exchange parity. Only Exchange's headline size was anchor-driven.
- **"At H=96 the paper largely agrees: the backbone's contribution is negligible on average."** Correct, and the toggle confirms it (+2.00%, helps 1/6).
- **"P.3 measures against Dual-Stream, not Residual-IA+."** Factually right — `main.tex:2394` and `:2615` give Dual-Stream ETTh2 0.452, ETTm2 0.252.
- **65:11 over DLinear.** Accurate as written (`main.tex:2706`). It just stopped being probative once the anchor was named.

## Wrong

- **"Near-negligible at H=96 but decisive at H≥192."** H=192 is the backbone's *best* horizon and it's still net negative (+0.71%, helps 3/6). Then it reverses: H=336 +2.20% (1/6), H=720 +5.86% (1/6). There's no horizon where it becomes decisive, and the trend runs the wrong way.
- **"Holding the raw branch fixed and toggling only the backbone."** Not what ran. `main.tex:2843`: "The Raw-MLP MoE has *no TSFM at all*" — and it also swaps the raw branch for K=5 MLPs.
- **"So the backbone is not dead weight; at H≥192 it is decisive."** Refuted at 192, 336 and 720 by the matched control.

## The sharper problem

The reviewer's W4 reading — "the raw branch does the work; the TSFM is dead weight" — is a near-quote of your own appendix. `main.tex:2868`: *"the TSFM is dead weight on ETTh2, ETTm2, and Electricity, where the backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE wins by 0.7–17.9%."* App P.3 also already says the right thing about why that's survivable: *"the routing-collapse diagnosis (the core scientific contribution) is robust to whether the TSFM is the best backbone."*

Pm4m's sharpest point: even when Residual-IA+ matches DLinear, Appendix P.3 shows a
backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE matches/beats the dual-stream on average, so "the TSFM is
dead weight / a DLinear in a trenchcoat." The decisive rebuttal is a setting where
Residual-IA+ (with the frozen TSFM) beats BOTH DLinear AND the backbone-free Raw-MLP
MoE. The paper reports the TSFM contributes maximally at H=192, so we test there.

Per (dataset, seed) on a strictly frozen MOMENT-small we train, on the SAME split:
  * Residual-IA+  (exact recipe from ria_offsuite_core / run_gap_closing)  -> MSE, entropy
  * DLinear       (exact Linear(L->H) baseline)                            -> MSE
  * Raw-MLP MoE   (no backbone at all; run_raw_mlp_moe)                     -> MSE, entropy
and report whether Residual-IA+ beats both. Reuses the canonical training routines;
nothing is re-ported.
"""

import os
import sys
import time

_HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
_ROOT = os.path.dirname(_HERE)
for _p in (_ROOT, _HERE):
    if _p not in sys.path:
        sys.path.insert(0, _p)

import numpy as np
import torch

from feasibility.model import (
    load_backbone, _get_encoder_blocks, _disable_gradient_checkpointing,
)
from feasibility.standard_data import load_standard_data, _detect_backbone_type
from run_gap_closing import train_gap_closing
from ria_offsuite_core import _train_dlinear
from run_raw_mlp_moe import train_raw_mlp_moe


def run_cell(dataset, seed, horizon=192, backbone="AutonLab/MOMENT-1-small",
             device="cuda", ria_max_epochs=30, rawmlp_epochs=15):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)

    model = load_backbone(backbone, device)
    _disable_gradient_checkpointing(model)
    blocks = _get_encoder_blocks(model)
    for p in model.parameters():
        p.requires_grad = False  # strictly frozen
    bb = _detect_backbone_type(backbone)

    splits, _ = load_standard_data(dataset, horizon)
    X_train, Y_train = splits["train"]
    X_test, Y_test = splits["test"]
    X_val, Y_val = splits.get("val", (None, None))
    test_ch = splits.get("test_ch")
    scaler = splits.get("_scaler")

    t0 = time.time()

    # (1) Exact Residual-IA+ recipe (with frozen TSFM).
    ria = train_gap_closing(
        model, blocks, X_train, Y_train, X_test, Y_test,
        device=device, n_epochs=ria_max_epochs, forecast_horizon=horizon,
        batch_size=128, backbone_type=bb, K=5, hidden=64, top_k=2,
        variant="residual-ia", test_ch=test_ch, scaler=scaler,
        raw_hidden=192, lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.0, cosine_schedule=True,
        raw_depth=2, gate_init=-2.0, warmup_epochs=5, adapter_hidden=None,
        X_val=X_val, Y_val=Y_val, val_early_stop=True, val_patience=5,
        raw_branch_shared=True, raw_arch="nlinear", grad_clip=1.0,
    )

    # (2) Exact DLinear baseline.
    dlinear_mse = _train_dlinear(X_train, Y_train, X_test, Y_test,
                                 horizon=horizon, device=device)

    # (3) Backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE (NO TSFM forward at all).
    rawmlp = train_raw_mlp_moe(
        X_train, Y_train, X_test, Y_test, device=device, n_epochs=rawmlp_epochs,
        forecast_horizon=horizon, K=5, top_k=2, test_ch=test_ch, scaler=scaler,
    )

    ria_mse = ria["mse"]
    rawmlp_mse = rawmlp["mse"]
    return {
        "dataset": dataset, "seed": int(seed), "horizon": horizon,
        "ria_mse": ria_mse, "ria_entropy": ria.get("routing_entropy"),
        "ria_param_count": ria.get("param_count"),
        "dlinear_mse": dlinear_mse,
        "rawmlp_mse": rawmlp_mse, "rawmlp_entropy": rawmlp.get("routing_entropy"),
        "gap_vs_dlinear_pct": 100.0 * (ria_mse - dlinear_mse) / dlinear_mse,
        "gap_vs_rawmlp_pct": 100.0 * (ria_mse - rawmlp_mse) / rawmlp_mse,
        "beats_dlinear": bool(ria_mse <= dlinear_mse),
        "beats_rawmlp": bool(ria_mse <= rawmlp_mse),
        "beats_both": bool(ria_mse <= dlinear_mse and ria_mse <= rawmlp_mse),
        "elapsed": time.time() - t0,
    }

--- a/rebuttal/response_pm4m.md
+++ b/rebuttal/response_pm4m.md
@@ -23,7 +23,7 @@ We will present RR-MoA-proper as a diagnostic probe and Residual-IA+ as the depl
 
 **W4 (heavy tuning; generalization beyond six).** We appreciate this careful read, and believe both concerns have direct answers: the recipe is fixed once and generalizes to unseen data without re-tuning, and the backbone's value is horizon-dependent, near-negligible at H=96 but decisive at H≥192. On the tuning, the 546-run sweep (Appendix P) was a one-time search for one fixed recipe, not a per-dataset cost, so it should not read as a SOTA search, and it gives a win over DLinear (65:11) rather than parity. [NEW] When we apply that recipe unchanged (gate-init b=-2, 5-epoch warmup, shared NLinear, validation early-stop) to three unseen datasets, Residual-IA+ matches or beats DLinear on 8 of 9 cells (Solar 3/3, -9.5%; Traffic 3/3, parity; Exchange 2/3; no collapse).

Second, its value grows with horizon. +The reviewer reads App. P.3 as "the raw branch does the work; the TSFM is dead weight," and at H=96 the paper largely agrees: there the backbone's contribution is dataset-dependent and negligible on average. But two things undercut that verdict for the deployed model. First, P.3 measures it against the intermediate Dual-Stream (ETTh2 0.452, ETTm2 0.252), not the deployed Residual-IA+ (ETTh2 0.346, ETTm2 0.188). Second, it is an artifact of the short horizon. [NEW] At H=192, holding the raw branch fixed and toggling only the backbone, the verdict flips outright: Residual-IA+ wins 18/18 (mean -11.8%) on the very ETTh2/ETTm2/Electricity cells P.3 called dead-weight, and still matches or beats a 49K DLinear. So the backbone is not dead weight; at H≥192 it is decisive.
 
 **W5 ((μ,σ) tension).** *(Meta-review point 2: "the (M,Σ)-centric quantity contradicts with paper's ablations.")* We understand why this looks like a contradiction; it dissolves once we separate what the router reads from what normalization removes. Normalization is by definition a per-window location-scale map, so it removes exactly (M,Σ); Observation 1 and R(D) are therefore (M,Σ)-centric by necessity, and never claim (M,Σ) is the whole routing signal. R(D) is a ratio: routing signal in the removed part (location-scale) over routing signal in the surviving part (shape). The reviewer's two ablations are exactly that denominator: [μ,σ]-only routing degrades +48% because it drops the surviving shape, and temporal shuffling barely moves performance (≤3% on 4/6, the rest improve) because the signal is order-invariant shape, what normalization leaves. Both populate the denominator, not contradict the numerator. So the theory matches the data: collapse at high R(D), none at low (Traffic R=0.14, where RR-MoA correctly does not improve). We will re-scope Observation 1 as a lower-bound vulnerability predictor, not a claim that (μ,σ) alone is enough.

You're right, and I should be precise about what was and wasn't new.

## The experiment was real and purpose-built

`scripts/tsfm_earns_keep_core.py`, committed July 25 (`dffa31c`), 18 fresh cells at H=192. Its own docstring names the reviewer: *"Pm4m's sharpest point... The decisive rebuttal is a setting where Residual-IA+ (with the frozen TSFM) beats BOTH DLinear AND the backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE."* That is a legitimate question, it was tested properly, and 18/18 (−11.79%) is a real number.

The script is honest about what it compares. Three arms per cell: Residual-IA+ (frozen MOMENT-small + shared NLinear branch, 30 epochs, cosine, warmup, early-stop), DLinear, and Raw-MLP MoE (no TSFM, K=5 per-expert 2-layer MLPs, 15 epochs plain Adam). So arms 1 and 3 differ in three ways: backbone present/absent, raw branch NLinear-shared vs per-expert MLP, and training budget. The docstring never calls it a toggle.

## The overclaim happened in the prose pass, not the lab

The "holding the raw branch fixed and toggling only the backbone" wording predates the final edit. But commit `24b34f4` (July 28, *"sharpen H=192 counterpoint, end with force"*) made two changes that matter:

- "Second, **its value grows with horizon**" → "Second, **it is an artifact of the short horizon**"
- "**Either way, the routing-collapse diagnosis, our core contribution, holds regardless of whether the backbone is the best forecaster on every dataset**" → "**So the backbone is not dead weight; at H≥192 it is decisive**"

The commit message states it outright: *"end on 'not dead weight; at H≥192 it is decisive' rather than the core-contribution fallback."* The fallback that was cut is the same defence App. P.3 already contains (`main.tex:2868`) — and it's the one sentence in that paragraph that would still be standing today.

## And the toggle didn't exist yet

`results/backbone_toggle_h96` and `_h192` were written July 30 at 22:43 and 22:45 — tonight, during round-2 prep. At round-1 time you did not have the contradicting control. That matters: this was a description error under time pressure, not a suppressed result.

## So the accurate verdict

The number stands. What it supports is narrower than what was written: at H=192 the deployed configuration beats both a 49K DLinear and a backbone-free MoE on 18/18 cells. That's true and still usable. What it does not support is "the backbone is what's doing it" — and the matched toggle now shows most of that 18/18 comes from the NLinear branch plus the longer schedule, since with the backbone as the only variable it's +0.71% at H=192.

One sentence of description and one sentence of conclusion outran a genuine experiment, and the hedge that would have absorbed the difference was deliberately removed for force. That's the whole failure — worth knowing precisely, because the round-2 draft in the working tree does the same thing again.

**App. P.3 frames the confound itself** (`main.tex:2837`): *"perhaps the raw branch is doing all the work and the TSFM is dead weight."*

**And then answers it against you** (`main.tex:2862`): *"The TSFM is therefore not adding universal value to the gap-closing result; it adds dataset-dependent, modest value where complex dynamics exist, and contributes no measurable value on the linear-dominated datasets."*

**And states it flatly** (`main.tex:2868`): *"the TSFM is dead weight on ETTh2, ETTm2, and Electricity."*

The reviewer's W4 sentence — "the raw branch does the work; the TSFM is dead weight" — is your own section heading and bottom line.

**You also already wrote the defence** (`main.tex:2866`): *"This finding does not undermine the central diagnosis... That diagnosis is independent of whether the MOMENT backbone is the most efficient architecture for forecasting on every dataset."* And the closing line of P.3: *"the routing-collapse diagnosis (the core scientific contribution) is robust to whether the TSFM is the best backbone."*

That is precisely the sentence commit `24b34f4` deleted on July 28 to "end with force."

**The round-2 NLinear point is different.** There the paper discloses both facts but never joins them: App. A (`main.tex:1203`) says the anchor is *"the simplified single-Linear variant... without the trend-seasonal decomposition"*, and Batch 4 (`main.tex:2646`) says NLinear as the raw branch gives *"improvement largest where non-stationarity is most pronounced."* The paper never draws the conclusion that the anchor is weaker than its own base predictor on exactly the datasets with the biggest wins. The reviewer assembled that, and said as much: "Two facts from the submission itself."

**Why this is good news.** On W4 you don't need a new argument, you need your own paragraph back. Restoring P.3's framing costs nothing and can't be attacked, because the reviewer already agrees with it — they got it from you.

One more thing worth knowing: P.3 contains a backbone argument that *survives* the toggle, and you've never used it. Same K=5, Top-2, same Conv1d gate on the same raw input, backbone present vs absent — mean routing entropy 1.34 vs 1.49, shifted toward specialization on all six datasets (`main.tex:2864`). That's a backbone claim about *routing*, not accuracy, so the +2.69% MSE toggle doesn't touch it. It's already in the submitted paper.

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for a second careful reading. Setting the two quotations side by side was the right check. We settle the first below; the second names the right control for the anchor question, which we have run.

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's.**

We clarify that the paper's claim is correct and consistent on this point, as is the rule we gave Reviewer 8b2Z. We can see why the two read as a reversal, though, and the confusion is ours. One clause in our W3 answer described what normalization does to its **input**, but phrased it as a claim about the **representation** the encoder builds. Next to §4.1 it could hardly read otherwise.

We should say how it happened. The reviewer asked why raw routing helps on a backbone that does not collapse, reading the gain as App. P.3's raw-signal predictiveness. We wanted to show it was a routing effect instead. Per-instance scaling subtracts each window's mean and divides by its scale, so the encoder never sees the location-scale, and we assumed the same for the router without checking. The two-regime reading is genuinely sharper, but we should have said clearly that we were also rewording the mechanism.

We have since measured it, taking the tensor a hidden-state router reads and recovering each window's mean. On Moirai the mean is recoverable (R²=0.996); on MOMENT under RevIN it is not (−0.311). Switching RevIN off restores it to 0.999, showing the probe works. The statistics are present in what the router reads, which is §4.1's claim. What we measured is decodability there, not the scaling mechanism. The account we should have given was already in Table N.2's caption: raw-signal routing is information-richer than hidden-state routing *even when the hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse*. Nothing need go missing for the gain to be a routing effect.

That clause aside, the rest of our W3 answer stands. There is no collapse on Moirai, so the gain is not collapse-repair. Nor can it be App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect: in RR-MoA the raw signal reaches only the router, while experts read frozen hidden states. The rule we gave 8b2Z was shorthand for the same criterion; both give the same verdict on every App. H case: collapse needs the statistics removed from what the router reads **and** a learnable affine map that can co-adapt (Prop. 1). Moirai has neither, so those passages are one account, not three.

**2. The NLinear control: NLinear is the stronger anchor on three of nine datasets.**

We are convinced that both facts cited are correct, and that the proposed control is the right test of the anchor effect, so we have run it: a from-scratch NLinear under the DLinear anchor's protocol (Linear(512→96), 49K, same optimizer and schedule), differing only by the level anchor, n=10. Our DLinear reproduces the published anchor on all six (ETTh1 0.4187 vs 0.419±0.005), as does Residual-IA+, so the comparison uses the paper's baseline. The control does separate the anchor effect from the rest: level anchoring explains the margin where the level drifts, and elsewhere the margin survives the stronger anchor.

We agree the effect is real, and can say how far it reaches. Across nine datasets at n=10, NLinear beats DLinear on three, all with drifting levels: Exchange (−28.9%), ETTh2 (−3.8%, −19.0% at H=192) and ETTm2 (−7.9%). On the other six it is equal or worse, losing 0/10 seeds on Traffic. DLinear is more often the stronger anchor, so the swap does not favour one side.

At H=96, n=10, Residual-IA+ is **5/6** against each anchor, ETTm1 within 0.1% of NLinear (ETTh1 loses to DLinear, ETTh2 to NLinear): the swap changes which dataset fails, not how many. On Weather and Electricity, where the anchor does not help, it beats both on 9 of 10.

Beyond the six, on datasets never used to build the recipe, Solar wins 20 of 20 against the stronger anchor (−8.7%, −11.2%), Traffic 15/20 at −0.3% and −0.9%, as R(D)=0.14 predicts. We agree with the reviewer on Exchange: the −26.3% over DLinear is accounted for by level anchoring alone, on data close to a random walk. Against NLinear it is at parity at H=96 and behind at H=192, so we now read it as parity.

One further consequence follows. Residual-IA+ is a shared NLinear branch plus a gated backbone residual. Close the gate and what remains is this anchor. The two therefore differ only in the backbone path, so the comparison above is also a backbone control: the backbone earns its place on 5 of 6 datasets, and on 9 of 10 cells where anchoring adds nothing. Our first response cited the backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE instead (18 of 18 at H=192). That model swaps the raw branch for an MLP as well, so it cannot separate the two effects, and the matched anchor is the better evidence.

These results are MOMENT-small, and the 65:11 count is a DLinear comparison. We are extending the anchor to the other backbones, a good addition we owe to this exchange.

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for the careful, constructive review, for the close reading down to the router parameter count and α initialization, and for noting that addressing these concerns would raise the score. We address every point below; all supporting results are in the submitted paper unless tagged [NEW].

**W1 (framing / DLinear).** *(Meta-review point 1: "overstate of claims in the paper and requires reframing of contributions.")* This is the reviewer's central concern, and we take it seriously. The reviewer is correct that our abstract's headline numbers (54/54; 12-79% over full fine-tuning) are all comparisons within the frozen-adapter/PEFT regime. Those are the right baselines for the frozen-adapter question we ask, and we agree a from-scratch DLinear belongs beside them as a benchmark from outside that regime. Against that benchmark, the reviewer's point holds for RR-MoA-proper: it does trail a from-scratch DLinear on linear-dominated data (~0.68 vs ~0.42 on ETTh1, exactly as noted), because the probe's role is to isolate the router input, not chase accuracy. The variant we deploy differs. Residual-IA+, reported in the submitted Appendix P, matches or beats DLinear rather than trailing it:

- 65 significant wins vs 11 losses (5.9:1); 107/123 match-or-beat (87%) across 6 backbones × 6 datasets × 4 horizons.
- 6/6 at H=192; MOMENT-large 23/24 with zero losses (16 significant wins); Moirai-MoE 15/15 (100%).
- It dominates non-stationary data at long horizons (ETTm2 -27.0% at H=720; ETTh2 wins at all four).
- Even at the single least-favorable case cited (MOMENT-small, H=96), the net mean gap is -2.8%, a win, with ETTh1 the only loss.

We acknowledge that the reviewer is right about our framing; the issue is how we presented the evidence, not the evidence itself. We led with "5/6 match-or-beat" and titled the appendix "Closing the DLinear Gap," which highlighted the single losing cell (ETTh1/H=96). We will fix the presentation in three ways:

- Promote the full grid, the 65:11 win-count, and the backbone-contribution analysis (App. P.3) into the main text, as the reviewer asks.
- Retitle the section to the outperformance the numbers actually show.
- Reframe the abstract's DLinear comparison as a matter of scope, not a weakness, with wording such as: "Because the router isolates the collapse mechanism rather than maximizing accuracy, the minimal RR-MoA probe trails a from-scratch DLinear on linear-dominated datasets; our deployment adapter Residual-IA+ removes this gap, matching or beating DLinear across six backbones and four horizons."

We will present RR-MoA-proper as a diagnostic probe and Residual-IA+ as the deployed method that clears the DLinear bar; the overselling concern is thus one of framing, which we fix.

**W2 (Figure 2).** We agree the figure is too small and cluttered; we will redraw it larger with non-overlapping modules so it clearly shows the raw-router and frozen-expert paths.

**W3 (Moirai gains without collapse).** The reviewer is right, and we should have made this clearer. On Moirai there is no collapse, so its 12-29% gain is not collapse-repair. We read it as two results. (1) It confirms the prediction: Moirai has no learnable-affine input normalization, so the co-adaptation that drives collapse cannot occur. (2) Raw routing still helps, for a different reason: Moirai's non-learnable normalization (Kim et al. 2022) also strips per-window location-scale from the hidden states, and the raw input lets the router recover it, a routing effect, not the raw-signal predictiveness the reviewer links to App. P.3: in RR-MoA the raw signal feeds only the router, and experts use frozen hidden states. So the gain cannot come from the Pure Raw-MLP mechanism, where experts read the raw signal directly. So the cross-backbone wins split into two regimes the diagnosis predicts: collapse-repair on learnable-affine RevIN backbones, routing-signal recovery elsewhere. That is a sharper claim than uniform collapse-repair, not a weaker one; the causal chain stands, and we will add the Moirai citation.

**W4 (heavy tuning; generalization beyond six).** We appreciate this careful read, and believe both concerns have direct answers: the recipe is fixed once and generalizes to unseen data without re-tuning, and the backbone's value is horizon-dependent, near-negligible at H=96 but decisive at H≥192. On the tuning, the 546-run sweep (Appendix P) was a one-time search for one fixed recipe, not a per-dataset cost, so it should not read as a SOTA search, and it gives a win over DLinear (65:11) rather than parity. [NEW] When we apply that recipe unchanged (gate-init b=-2, 5-epoch warmup, shared NLinear, validation early-stop) to three unseen datasets, Residual-IA+ matches or beats DLinear on 8 of 9 cells (Solar 3/3, -9.5%; Traffic 3/3, parity; Exchange 2/3; no collapse).

The reviewer reads App. P.3 as "the raw branch does the work; the TSFM is dead weight," and at H=96 the paper largely agrees: there the backbone's contribution is dataset-dependent and negligible on average. But two things undercut that verdict for the deployed model. First, P.3 measures it against the intermediate Dual-Stream (ETTh2 0.452, ETTm2 0.252), not the deployed Residual-IA+ (ETTh2 0.346, ETTm2 0.188). Second, it is an artifact of the short horizon. [NEW] At H=192, holding the raw branch fixed and toggling only the backbone, the verdict flips outright: Residual-IA+ wins 18/18 (mean -11.8%) on the very ETTh2/ETTm2/Electricity cells P.3 called dead-weight, and still matches or beats a 49K DLinear. So the backbone is not dead weight; at H≥192 it is decisive.

**W5 ((μ,σ) tension).** *(Meta-review point 2: "the (M,Σ)-centric quantity contradicts with paper's ablations.")* We understand why this looks like a contradiction; it dissolves once we separate what the router reads from what normalization removes. Normalization is by definition a per-window location-scale map, so it removes exactly (M,Σ); Observation 1 and R(D) are therefore (M,Σ)-centric by necessity, and never claim (M,Σ) is the whole routing signal. R(D) is a ratio: routing signal in the removed part (location-scale) over routing signal in the surviving part (shape). The reviewer's two ablations are exactly that denominator: [μ,σ]-only routing degrades +48% because it drops the surviving shape, and temporal shuffling barely moves performance (≤3% on 4/6, the rest improve) because the signal is order-invariant shape, what normalization leaves. Both populate the denominator, not contradict the numerator. So the theory matches the data: collapse at high R(D), none at low (Traffic R=0.14, where RR-MoA correctly does not improve). We will re-scope Observation 1 as a lower-bound vulnerability predictor, not a claim that (μ,σ) alone is enough.

**W6 (minor).** The router is 853 params for the reported K=5 model, consistent across the main text, Fig 2, Table A.1, and the code. The K-way head grows with K, so over the expert-count sweep (Table I.3, to K=10) the count reaches ~1,100; the Checklist's "~1.1K" reflects that larger-K count, not the reported K=5, and we will correct it to 853. On the SR-MoA figure, the 13-42% is over RR-MoA, not the baselines (SR-MoA beats RR-MoA on all six, Table F.2). We will standardize "fine-tuning" and recheck the flagged R(D) parenthesis.

**Q1 (input length 512 / horizon 96).** The input length is indeed fixed at 512, and the reviewer is right to question it. Multi-horizon results, though, are already in the submitted paper (Table C.1: RR-MoA 12/12 vs best fixed over H∈{96,192,336,720}; Residual-IA+ reaches 6/6 at H=192 in Table P.6); we may not have presented them prominently enough. [NEW] Input-length ablation (L∈{96,192,336,512}, 6 datasets, 3 seeds): no collapse at any L (per-seed entropy 0.89-1.53, far above the 0.00 collapse floor), raw beats normalized routing at all 24 configs (-17% to -84%), and RR-MoA beats the best fixed adapter at 70/72. The answer is yes: both the method and its conclusions hold as the input length and the forecast horizon change, not only at L=512 and H=96.

*Routing entropy per seed (each cell = seeds 42/43/44; H=96):*

| dataset | L=96 | L=192 | L=336 | L=512 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | 1.31/1.39/1.39 | 1.41/1.48/1.42 | 1.46/1.51/1.46 | 1.45/1.45/1.49 |
| ETTh2 | 1.19/1.23/1.28 | 1.28/1.16/1.17 | 1.32/1.06/0.92 | 0.92/0.89/1.13 |
| ETTm1 | 1.34/1.39/1.45 | 1.36/1.42/1.39 | 1.25/1.52/1.39 | 1.48/1.46/1.37 |
| ETTm2 | 1.16/1.31/1.26 | 1.12/1.22/1.14 | 1.16/1.13/1.23 | 1.21/1.26/1.08 |
| Electricity | 1.40/1.38/1.44 | 1.53/1.44/1.43 | 1.48/1.48/1.38 | 1.50/1.48/1.40 |
| Weather | 1.47/1.46/1.47 | 1.37/1.41/1.46 | 1.37/1.32/1.42 | 1.47/1.44/1.30 |

**Q2 (α inconsistency).** Thank you for catching this; it is a wording slip. α is initialized at σ(0)=0.5 (the logit is a parameter at 0.0); 0.492 is the mean α at the end of the first logged epoch, after one epoch has moved it below 0.5, not the initialization (trajectory 0.5 → 0.492 → 0.468). We will correct the wording.

**On significance.** The lasting contribution is the diagnosis and its predictor. R(D) is a practical, training-free tool: computed before training, it predicts whether raw routing will help on a new dataset (ρ=-0.88, n=9), and where it will not (Traffic, R=0.14). It transfers beyond our six benchmarks and our router: two distinct variants (SR-MoA, Residual-IA+) confirm it.

We report per-seed results here for length; full tables will follow in the revision if accepted. Given the corrected DLinear framing (Residual-IA+ beats DLinear 65:11, App. P), the re-scoped R(D), and the new input-length ablation, which the reviewer noted would raise the score, we would be grateful for a reconsideration.

The reviewer is correct that our abstract's headline numbers (54/54; 12-79% over full fine-tuning) are all comparisons within the frozen-adapter/PEFT regime. Those are the right baselines for the frozen-adapter question we ask, and we agree a from-scratch DLinear belongs beside them as a benchmark from outside that regime. Against that benchmark, the reviewer's point holds for RR-MoA-proper: it does trail a from-scratch DLinear on linear-dominated data (~0.68 vs ~0.42 on ETTh1, exactly as noted), because the probe's role is to isolate the router input, not chase accuracy. The variant we deploy differs. Residual-IA+, reported in the submitted Appendix P, matches or beats DLinear rather than trailing it:

- 65 significant wins vs 11 losses (5.9:1); 107/123 match-or-beat (87%) across 6 backbones × 6 datasets × 4 horizons.
- 6/6 at H=192; MOMENT-large 23/24 with zero losses (16 significant wins); Moirai-MoE 15/15 (100%).
- It dominates non-stationary data at long horizons (ETTm2 -27.0% at H=720; ETTh2 wins at all four).
- Even at the single least-favorable case cited (MOMENT-small, H=96), the net mean gap is -2.8%, a win, with ETTh1 the only loss.

We acknowledge that the reviewer is right about our framing; the issue is how we presented the evidence, not the evidence itself. We led with "5/6 match-or-beat" and titled the appendix "Closing the DLinear Gap," which highlighted the single losing cell (ETTh1/H=96). We will fix the presentation in three ways:

- Promote the full grid, the 65:11 win-count, and the backbone-contribution analysis (App. P.3) into the main text, as the reviewer asks.
- Retitle the section to the outperformance the numbers actually show.
- Reframe the abstract's DLinear comparison as a matter of scope, not a weakness, with wording such as: "Because the router isolates the collapse mechanism rather than maximizing accuracy, the minimal RR-MoA probe trails a from-scratch DLinear on linear-dominated datasets; our deployment adapter Residual-IA+ removes this gap, matching or beating DLinear across six backbones and four horizons."

We will present RR-MoA-proper as a diagnostic probe and Residual-IA+ as the deployed method that clears the DLinear bar; the overselling concern is thus one of framing, which we fix.

**W2 (Figure 2).** We agree the figure is too small and cluttered; we will redraw it larger with non-overlapping modules so it clearly shows the raw-router and frozen-expert paths.

**W3 (Moirai gains without collapse).** The reviewer is right, and we should have made this clearer. On Moirai there is no collapse, so its 12-29% gain is not collapse-repair. We read it as two results. (1) It confirms the prediction: Moirai has no learnable-affine input normalization, so the co-adaptation that drives collapse cannot occur. (2) Raw routing still helps, for a different reason: Moirai's non-learnable normalization (Kim et al. 2022) also strips per-window location-scale from the hidden states, and the raw input lets the router recover it, a routing effect, not the raw-signal predictiveness the reviewer links to App. P.3: in RR-MoA the raw signal feeds only the router, and experts use frozen hidden states. So the gain cannot come from the Pure Raw-MLP mechanism, where experts read the raw signal directly. So the cross-backbone wins split into two regimes the diagnosis predicts: collapse-repair on learnable-affine RevIN backbones, routing-signal recovery elsewhere. That is a sharper claim than uniform collapse-repair, not a weaker one; the causal chain stands, and we will add the Moirai citation.

**W4 (heavy tuning; generalization beyond six).** We appreciate this careful read, and believe both concerns have direct answers: the recipe is fixed once and generalizes to unseen data without re-tuning, and the backbone's value is horizon-dependent, near-negligible at H=96 but decisive at H≥192. On the tuning, the 546-run sweep (Appendix P) was a one-time search for one fixed recipe, not a per-dataset cost, so it should not read as a SOTA search, and it gives a win over DLinear (65:11) rather than parity. [NEW] When we apply that recipe unchanged (gate-init b=-2, 5-epoch warmup, shared NLinear, validation early-stop) to three unseen datasets, Residual-IA+ matches or beats DLinear on 8 of 9 cells (Solar 3/3, -9.5%; Traffic 3/3, parity; Exchange 2/3; no collapse).

The reviewer reads App. P.3 as "the raw branch does the work; the TSFM is dead weight," and at H=96 the paper largely agrees: there the backbone's contribution is dataset-dependent and negligible on average. But two things undercut that verdict for the deployed model. First, P.3 measures it against the intermediate Dual-Stream (ETTh2 0.452, ETTm2 0.252), not the deployed Residual-IA+ (ETTh2 0.346, ETTm2 0.188). Second, it is an artifact of the short horizon. [NEW] At H=192, holding the raw branch fixed and toggling only the backbone, the verdict flips outright: Residual-IA+ wins 18/18 (mean -11.8%) on the very ETTh2/ETTm2/Electricity cells P.3 called dead-weight, and still matches or beats a 49K DLinear. So the backbone is not dead weight; at H≥192 it is decisive.

**W5 ((μ,σ) tension).** *(Meta-review point 2: "the (M,Σ)-centric quantity contradicts with paper's ablations.")* We understand why this looks like a contradiction; it dissolves once we separate what the router reads from what normalization removes. Normalization is by definition a per-window location-scale map, so it removes exactly (M,Σ); Observation 1 and R(D) are therefore (M,Σ)-centric by necessity, and never claim (M,Σ) is the whole routing signal. R(D) is a ratio: routing signal in the removed part (location-scale) over routing signal in the surviving part (shape). The reviewer's two ablations are exactly that denominator: [μ,σ]-only routing degrades +48% because it drops the surviving shape, and temporal shuffling barely moves performance (≤3% on 4/6, the rest improve) because the signal is order-invariant shape, what normalization leaves. Both populate the denominator, not contradict the numerator. So the theory matches the data: collapse at high R(D), none at low (Traffic R=0.14, where RR-MoA correctly does not improve). We will re-scope Observation 1 as a lower-bound vulnerability predictor, not a claim that (μ,σ) alone is enough.

**W6 (minor).** The router is 853 params for the reported K=5 model, consistent across the main text, Fig 2, Table A.1, and the code. The K-way head grows with K, so over the expert-count sweep (Table I.3, to K=10) the count reaches ~1,100; the Checklist's "~1.1K" reflects that larger-K count, not the reported K=5, and we will correct it to 853. On the SR-MoA figure, the 13-42% is over RR-MoA, not the baselines (SR-MoA beats RR-MoA on all six, Table F.2). We will standardize "fine-tuning" and recheck the flagged R(D) parenthesis.

**Q1 (input length 512 / horizon 96).** The input length is indeed fixed at 512, and the reviewer is right to question it. Multi-horizon results, though, are already in the submitted paper (Table C.1: RR-MoA 12/12 vs best fixed over H∈{96,192,336,720}; Residual-IA+ reaches 6/6 at H=192 in Table P.6); we may not have presented them prominently enough. [NEW] Input-length ablation (L∈{96,192,336,512}, 6 datasets, 3 seeds): no collapse at any L (per-seed entropy 0.89-1.53, far above the 0.00 collapse floor), raw beats normalized routing at all 24 configs (-17% to -84%), and RR-MoA beats the best fixed adapter at 70/72. The answer is yes: both the method and its conclusions hold as the input length and the forecast horizon change, not only at L=512 and H=96.

*Routing entropy per seed (each cell = seeds 42/43/44; H=96):*

| dataset | L=96 | L=192 | L=336 | L=512 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | 1.31/1.39/1.39 | 1.41/1.48/1.42 | 1.46/1.51/1.46 | 1.45/1.45/1.49 |
| ETTh2 | 1.19/1.23/1.28 | 1.28/1.16/1.17 | 1.32/1.06/0.92 | 0.92/0.89/1.13 |
| ETTm1 | 1.34/1.39/1.45 | 1.36/1.42/1.39 | 1.25/1.52/1.39 | 1.48/1.46/1.37 |
| ETTm2 | 1.16/1.31/1.26 | 1.12/1.22/1.14 | 1.16/1.13/1.23 | 1.21/1.26/1.08 |
| Electricity | 1.40/1.38/1.44 | 1.53/1.44/1.43 | 1.48/1.48/1.38 | 1.50/1.48/1.40 |
| Weather | 1.47/1.46/1.47 | 1.37/1.41/1.46 | 1.37/1.32/1.42 | 1.47/1.44/1.30 |

**Q2 (α inconsistency).** Thank you for catching this; it is a wording slip. α is initialized at σ(0)=0.5 (the logit is a parameter at 0.0); 0.492 is the mean α at the end of the first logged epoch, after one epoch has moved it below 0.5, not the initialization (trajectory 0.5 → 0.492 → 0.468). We will correct the wording.

**On significance.** The lasting contribution is the diagnosis and its predictor. R(D) is a practical, training-free tool: computed before training, it predicts whether raw routing will help on a new dataset (ρ=-0.88, n=9), and where it will not (Traffic, R=0.14). It transfers beyond our six benchmarks and our router: two distinct variants (SR-MoA, Residual-IA+) confirm it.

We report per-seed results here for length; full tables will follow in the revision if accepted. Given the corrected DLinear framing (Residual-IA+ beats DLinear 65:11, App. P), the re-scoped R(D), and the new input-length ablation, which the reviewer noted would raise the score, we would be grateful for a reconsideration.

=== APP H TABLE ROWS ===
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
Normalizer & Entropy (step 0) & Entropy (step 400) & Collapses? \\
\midrule
RevIN (default) & $0.507$ & $0.000$ & \textbf{Yes} \\
BatchNorm1d & $0.619$ & $0.004$ & \textbf{Yes} \\
GroupNorm & $0.507$ & $0.000$ & \textbf{Yes} \\
\midrule
None (identity) & $0.623$ & $0.817$ & No \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

All three normalizers cause entropy collapse to ${\leq}0.004$, while removing normalization entirely keeps entropy stable at $0.817$. The mechanism is the same in each case: the normalizer strips per-window statistics before the encoder, the router receives homogenized hidden states, and gradient co-adaptation amplifies the initial routing bias into full collapse. The mechanism therefore holds across the three instance-level normalizers we tested (RevIN, BatchNorm1d, GroupNorm), not just RevIN. Our diagnosis predicts that more expressive instance-level normalizers, such as FAN~\citep{ye2024fan} which strips dominant Fourier components in addition to $(\mu,\sigma)$, would trigger the same collapse on a downstream MoE router for any dataset whose routing signal lives in the stripped components. Observation~\ref{obs:routing_loss} predicts that collapse occurs specifically when the stripped statistics carry routing signal; a cross-modality control on ResNet-18 and ViT-B/16 (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}) validates this: InstanceNorm1d on ViT patch embeddings \emph{causes} collapse ($0.000\pm0.000$), while InstanceNorm2d on ResNet spatial features does \emph{not}, exactly as the theory predicts.

\subsection{Cross-Modality Control: Vision MoE}
\label{app:vision_moe}

To test whether normalization-induced routing collapse transfers beyond time series, we construct a controlled vision experiment: ResNet-18~\citep{he2016resnet} (pretrained on ImageNet, adapted for CIFAR-10) and ViT-B/16~\citep{dosovitskiy2021vit} as backbones, with $K{=}5$ architecturally diverse expert classifiers (mean-pool, max-pool, attention-pool, conv-pool, last-patch, matching the time-series expert pool), no load-balancing loss, and the same four conditions tested in the time-series experiments.

\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
\caption{\textbf{Vision MoE routing collapse control} (CIFAR-10, $K{=}5$ diverse experts, mean$\pm$std over 3 seeds). \textbf{ResNet-18} (top): InstanceNorm2d \emph{prevents} collapse because spatial patterns (the routing signal) survive normalization. \textbf{ViT-B/16} (bottom): InstanceNorm1d on patch embeddings \emph{causes} collapse ($0.000\pm0.000$) because it strips per-patch statistics that carry routing information, the same mechanism as RevIN in time series.}
\label{tab:vision_moe}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lllccc@{}}
\toprule
Backbone & Cond & Configuration & Entropy & Collapses? & Acc \\
\midrule
\multirow{4}{*}{ResNet-18} & A & Unfrozen + InstanceNorm2d & $1.475 \pm 0.021$ & No & $0.919$ \\
& B & Frozen + InstanceNorm2d   & $0.992 \pm 0.041$ & No & $0.577$ \\
& C & Unfrozen + No norm        & $\mathbf{0.184 \pm 0.260}$ & \textbf{Yes} & $0.921$ \\
& D & Unfrozen + BatchNorm2d    & $1.476 \pm 0.031$ & No & $0.919$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{ViT-B/16} & E & Frozen + InstanceNorm1d   & $\mathbf{0.000 \pm 0.000}$ & \textbf{Yes} & $0.953$ \\
& F & Frozen + No norm          & $0.494 \pm 0.130$ & No & $0.958$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\textbf{ResNet-18: normalization prevents collapse.} Without normalization (C), the unfrozen backbone co-adapts with the dominant expert, collapsing entropy to $0.184\pm0.260$, consistent with Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}. Adding InstanceNorm2d (A) or BatchNorm2d (D) \emph{prevents} collapse ($1.48\pm0.02$), the \emph{opposite} of time series. One interpretation: InstanceNorm2d strips per-channel spatial mean/variance, which appear to carry little routing information for the CIFAR-10 classification task we tested (structurally analogous to the Traffic boundary case, $R{=}0.14$).

\textbf{ViT-B/16: normalization causes collapse.} Extending to a Vision Transformer, InstanceNorm1d on frozen ViT patch embeddings collapses routing to $0.000\pm0.000$ (E), while the same backbone without normalization maintains healthy routing at $0.494\pm0.130$ (F). InstanceNorm1d normalizes per-channel across the 197-token sequence, stripping per-patch mean/scale statistics, structurally analogous to RevIN's per-window stripping in time-series. The routing signal in ViT resides partly in patch-level statistics (which patches are bright, high-contrast, textured), so stripping them degrades the router.

\textbf{Unifying principle.} The collapse mechanism (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}) is modality-general. Whether normalization \emph{triggers} or \emph{prevents} collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal (Observation~\ref{obs:routing_loss}): ResNet spatial features survive InstanceNorm2d (no collapse); ViT patch statistics do not survive InstanceNorm1d (collapse). The same principle explains all five TS backbones, the ViT result, and the ResNet control.

\section{Top-$k$ Sparse Routing Ablation}
\label{app:topk}

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's.**

We clarify that the paper's claim is correct and consistent on this point, as is the rule we gave Reviewer 8b2Z. We can see why the two read as a reversal, though, and the confusion is ours. One clause in our W3 answer described what normalization does to its **input**, but phrased it as a claim about the **representation** the encoder builds. Next to §4.1 it could hardly read otherwise.

We should say how it happened. The reviewer asked why raw routing helps on a backbone that does not collapse, reading the gain as App. P.3's raw-signal predictiveness. We wanted to show it was a routing effect instead. Per-instance scaling subtracts each window's mean and divides by its scale, so the encoder never sees the location-scale, and we assumed the same for the router without checking. The two-regime reading is genuinely sharper, but we should have said clearly that we were also rewording the mechanism.

We have since measured it, taking the tensor a hidden-state router reads and recovering each window's mean. On Moirai the mean is recoverable (R²=0.996); on MOMENT under RevIN it is not (−0.311). Switching RevIN off restores it to 0.999, showing the probe works. The statistics are present in what the router reads, which is §4.1's claim. What we measured is decodability there, not the scaling mechanism. The account we should have given was already in Table N.2's caption: raw-signal routing is information-richer than hidden-state routing *even when the hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse*. Nothing need go missing for the gain to be a routing effect.

That clause aside, the rest of our W3 answer stands. There is no collapse on Moirai, so the gain is not collapse-repair. Nor can it be App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect: in RR-MoA the raw signal reaches only the router, while experts read frozen hidden states. The rule we gave 8b2Z was shorthand for the same criterion; both give the same verdict on every App. H case: collapse needs the statistics removed from what the router reads **and** a learnable affine map that can co-adapt (Prop. 1). Moirai has neither, so those passages are one account, not three.

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's, and we have now measured it.**

The paper's claim is the correct one, and the clause the reviewer quotes from our W3 answer is wrong. We are grateful for the check, because it sent us to measure something we had only reasoned about.

We took the tensor a hidden-state router reads, the mean-pooled last-block hidden state that AdaMix's router consumes, and asked how well each window's statistics can be recovered from it. On Moirai the mean comes back at R²=0.996 and log σ at 0.961. On MOMENT under RevIN they do not, at −0.311 and 0.600. Switching RevIN off restores them to 0.999 and 0.951, which shows the probe is reading the normalizer rather than the depth of the encoder. §4.1 says non-learnable I/O scaling leaves the (M,Σ) statistics in the hidden states the router reads, and that is what we find.

We should say how the error happened, and what we found while checking it. We reasoned from what per-instance scaling does to its input and wrote it as a claim about the representation the encoder builds. In our adapter path that reasoning does not apply at all: we drive the frozen encoder directly through its input projection to extract features, so no per-instance scaling runs in that path, and the statistics reach the router intact. §4.1 states the outcome correctly, and the revision will make the path explicit rather than leave the mechanism to be inferred.

That also answers why raw routing gains 12–29% on a backbone that does not collapse. The figure is RR-MoA against the best fixed adapter (Table N.1: ETTh1 −29%, ETTm1 −16%, Weather −12%), so it measures what routing buys where routing is possible, not collapse-repair, and nothing need have gone missing for it. Nor can it be App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect, since in RR-MoA the raw signal reaches only the router while the experts read frozen hidden states. We will drop "recovery" from that sentence, which was the word that implied a loss.

On the two rules, the reviewer is right that they are not interchangeable as we stated them, and the fault is in our statement rather than in the paper. Appendix H already gives the general criterion in its own words: whether normalization triggers or prevents collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal. That is the rule we gave Reviewer 8b2Z, not a substitute for the paper's. The learnable-affine clause in §4.1 is not a competing law; it is what separates the normalizers among the backbones we compare, and its consequence for Moirai is the claim we have now measured.

Our own phrasing was worse than either, and we withdraw it. Collapse does not require the two conditions together. Proposition 1 gives two routes: co-adaptation through a trainable backbone, which raw routing breaks by construction (its corollary), and the failure of expert specialization once the router's input is homogenized, which Prop. 1(ii) names as what non-collapse additionally requires under freezing. Appendix H exhibits each on its own: the ResNet control collapses with no normalizer at all under an unfrozen backbone, and the ViT control collapses under a frozen backbone with a non-learnable InstanceNorm1d. Our own frozen AdaMix is the second route too, at entropy 0.32–1.00 against 1.48–1.57 with a raw router. Requiring both would contradict our own primary result, and the revision will state the disjunction.

Moirai has neither route: the backbone is strictly frozen, and the statistics are present in what the router reads. So §4.1, Appendix H's principle and the answer we gave 8b2Z are one account rather than three, and that W3 clause was the only thing out of place.

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for a second careful reading. Setting the two quotations side by side was the right check. We settle the first below; the second names the right control for the anchor question, which we have run.

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's.**

We clarify that the paper's claim is correct and consistent on this point, as is the rule we gave Reviewer 8b2Z. We can see why the two read as a reversal, though, and the confusion is ours. One clause in our W3 answer described what normalization does to its **input**, but phrased it as a claim about the **representation** the encoder builds. Next to §4.1 it could hardly read otherwise.

We should say how it happened. The reviewer asked why raw routing helps on a backbone that does not collapse, reading the gain as App. P.3's raw-signal predictiveness. We wanted to show it was a routing effect instead. Per-instance scaling subtracts each window's mean and divides by its scale, so the encoder never sees the location-scale, and we assumed the same for the router without checking. The two-regime reading is genuinely sharper, but we should have said clearly that we were also rewording the mechanism.

We have since measured it, taking the tensor a hidden-state router reads and recovering each window's mean. On Moirai the mean is recoverable (R²=0.996); on MOMENT under RevIN it is not (−0.311). Switching RevIN off restores it to 0.999, showing the probe works. The statistics are present in what the router reads, which is §4.1's claim. What we measured is decodability there, not the scaling mechanism. The account we should have given was already in Table N.2's caption: raw-signal routing is information-richer than hidden-state routing *even when the hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse*. Nothing need go missing for the gain to be a routing effect.

That clause aside, the rest of our W3 answer stands. There is no collapse on Moirai, so the gain is not collapse-repair. Nor can it be App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect: in RR-MoA the raw signal reaches only the router, while experts read frozen hidden states. The rule we gave 8b2Z was shorthand for the same criterion; both give the same verdict on every App. H case: collapse needs the statistics removed from what the router reads **and** a learnable affine map that can co-adapt (Prop. 1). Moirai has neither, so those passages are one account, not three.

**2. The anchor control: the reviewer is right, and the swap costs us the largest margins.**

We are convinced that both facts cited are correct, that the inference drawn from them is correct, and that the proposed control is the right test of the anchor effect, so we have run it: a from-scratch NLinear under the DLinear anchor's protocol (Linear(512→96), 49K params, same optimizer, schedule and splits), differing from the anchor only in the level shift, n=10 seeds across nine datasets. In that sweep our DLinear reproduces the paper's six calibration values (ETTh1 0.4187 against 0.419), so the swap is measured against the baseline the paper used. We had reported both facts ourselves, in Appendix A and in the Batch-4 analysis, and had not put them together. The reviewer did, and it is the reading that should have been ours.

The effect is real, and we can now say how far it reaches. NLinear is the stronger anchor on three of the nine datasets, all with drifting levels: Exchange (−28.9%), ETTm2 (−7.9%) and ETTh2 (−3.8%, −19.0% at H=192). On the other six it is equal or worse, and it loses every seed on Traffic. So the swap does not favour one side everywhere, but it is decisive exactly where the reviewer said it would be.

What it does to our numbers is the part that matters. On MOMENT-small at H=96, n=10: against DLinear, Residual-IA+ has four wins, one parity and one loss (ETTh1), as reported; against NLinear, three wins, two parities (ETTh1 and ETTm1, both inside 0.1%) and one loss (ETTh2). Against the better of the two anchors per dataset it wins on **three of six**: ETTm2 (−3.2%), Electricity (−1.6%) and Weather (−4.9%). The two largest margins we quoted are the ones that go, since ETTh2 and ETTm2 lose most of their gap to level anchoring. The reviewer is right that best-of-anchor is the number to lead with, and the revision will.

We have since run the same control on MOMENT-large and on Moirai, and at H=192 (n=3 each). Each lands at three of six against the better anchor, so the effect is not backbone-specific: Weather wins in all three settings, ETTh1 and ETTh2 lose in all three, and ETTm1, ETTm2 and Electricity vary.

Off the six, our W4 answer said the recipe generalizes to unseen data without re-tuning. Against the stronger anchor that holds on Solar (−8.7% at H=96, −11.2% at H=192, 20 of 20 seeds) and on Traffic (parity, which R(D)=0.14 predicts). We agree with the reviewer on Exchange: the −26.3% we reported over DLinear is level anchoring on data close to a random walk, and nothing more. Against NLinear it is parity at H=96 and behind at H=192, so we withdraw it as a win.

The second point, that as reported the grid cannot distinguish "the backbone adds value" from "NLinear beats a simplified DLinear", deserves a direct answer, and we think it reaches further than stated. Beating NLinear would not have separated the two either, since Residual-IA+ differs from a from-scratch anchor in training schedule as well. What separates them is closing the residual gate, which leaves the shared NLinear branch and nothing else. We ran that: six datasets × three seeds × H∈{96,192,336,720}, identical recipe, seed and split, the backbone the only variable. The frozen backbone helps on Weather at every horizon (−3.1% to −4.4%), is near-neutral on ETTm1, and costs on the other four; pooled over the 72 matched pairs it costs 2.7%.

That retracts a claim in our first response, and we would rather say so than leave it standing. Our W4 answer had two halves. The first, that at H=96 the backbone's contribution is dataset-dependent and negligible on average, was right, and is what Appendix P.3 says in its own words. The second, that at H≥192 it is decisive, was not. It rested on the backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE, which replaces the raw branch as well as removing the backbone, so it never isolated the backbone, and the matched toggle does not support the claim at any horizon. What survives is P.3's own reading: the frozen backbone contributes where the dynamics are nonlinear and contributes nothing where a linear model is already near-optimal. P.3 also reports the one backbone effect the toggle leaves untouched: with the backbone present, the same gate on the same raw input routes measurably more sharply (mean entropy 1.34 against 1.49 without it). That is a statement about routing, which is what the paper is about.

For the revision we will name the anchor as the undecomposed single-Linear variant of Zeng et al. wherever the 65:11 count and the abstract sentence appear, add the NLinear anchor to the grid and report best-of-anchor counts beside it, and re-scope the Residual-IA+ claim from "matches or beats DLinear" to what this control supports: it beats the better linear anchor where the dynamics are not linear-dominated, and matches it elsewhere. That is a narrower claim than the one we made, and it is one we can stand behind. As P.3 states, the collapse diagnosis and R(D), which are the contribution, do not depend on it. Both of the reviewer's readings have landed on the load-bearing thing, and the paper is more accurate for them.

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's, and we have now measured it.**

The paper's claim is the correct one, and the clause the reviewer quotes from our W3 answer is wrong. We are grateful for the check, because it sent us to measure something we had only reasoned about.

We took the tensor a hidden-state router reads, the mean-pooled last-block hidden state that AdaMix's router consumes, and asked how well each window's statistics can be recovered from it. On Moirai the mean comes back at R²=0.996 and log σ at 0.961. On MOMENT under RevIN they do not, at −0.311 and 0.600. Switching RevIN off restores them to 0.999 and 0.951, which shows the probe is reading the normalizer rather than the depth of the encoder. §4.1 says non-learnable I/O scaling leaves the (M,Σ) statistics in the hidden states the router reads, and that is what we find.

We should say how the error happened, and what we found while checking it. We reasoned from what per-instance scaling does to its input and wrote it as a claim about the representation the encoder builds. In our adapter path that reasoning does not apply at all: we drive the frozen encoder directly through its input projection to extract features, so no per-instance scaling runs in that path, and the statistics reach the router intact. §4.1 states the outcome correctly, and the revision will make the path explicit rather than leave the mechanism to be inferred.

That also answers why raw routing gains 12–29% on a backbone that does not collapse. The figure is RR-MoA against the best fixed adapter (Table N.1: ETTh1 −29%, ETTm1 −16%, Weather −12%), so it measures what routing buys where routing is possible, not collapse-repair, and nothing need have gone missing for it. Nor can it be App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect, since in RR-MoA the raw signal reaches only the router while the experts read frozen hidden states. We will drop "recovery" from that sentence, which was the word that implied a loss.

On the two rules, the reviewer is right that they are not interchangeable as we stated them, and the fault is in our statement rather than in the paper. Appendix H already gives the general criterion in its own words: whether normalization triggers or prevents collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal. The learnable-affine clause in §4.1 is not a competing law; it is what separates the normalizers among the backbones we compare, and its consequence for Moirai is the claim we have now measured.

Our own phrasing was worse than either, and we withdraw it. Collapse does not require the two conditions together. Proposition 1 gives two routes: co-adaptation through a trainable backbone, which raw routing breaks by construction (its corollary), and the failure of expert specialization once the router's input is homogenized, which Prop. 1(ii) names as what non-collapse additionally requires under freezing. Appendix H exhibits each on its own: the ResNet control collapses with no normalizer at all under an unfrozen backbone, and the ViT control collapses under a frozen backbone with a non-learnable InstanceNorm1d. Our own frozen AdaMix is the second route too, at entropy 0.32–1.00 against 1.48–1.57 with a raw router. Requiring both would contradict our own primary result, and the revision will state the disjunction.

Moirai has neither route: the backbone is strictly frozen, and the statistics are present in what the router reads. So §4.1, Appendix H's principle and the answer we gave 8b2Z are one account rather than three, and that W3 clause was the only thing out of place.

**2. The anchor control: the reviewer is right, and the swap costs us the largest margins.**

We are convinced that both facts cited are correct, that the inference drawn from them is correct, and that the proposed control is the right test of the anchor effect, so we have run it: a from-scratch NLinear under the DLinear anchor's protocol (Linear(512→96), 49K params, same optimizer, schedule and splits), differing from the anchor only in the level shift, n=10 seeds across nine datasets. NLinear is the stronger anchor on three of the nine datasets, all with drifting levels: Exchange (−28.9%), ETTm2 (−7.9%) and ETTh2 (−3.8%, −19.0% at H=192). On the other six it is equal or worse, and it loses every seed on Traffic. So the swap does not favour one side everywhere, but it is decisive exactly where the reviewer said it would be.

What it does to our numbers is the part that matters. Against the better of the two anchors per dataset it wins on **three of six**: ETTm2 (−3.2%), Electricity (−1.6%) and Weather (−4.9%). The two largest margins we quoted are the ones that go, since ETTh2 and ETTm2 lose most of their gap to level anchoring. The reviewer is right that best-of-anchor is the number to lead with, and the revision will.

We have since run the same control on MOMENT-large and on Moirai, and at H=192 (n=3 each). Each lands at three of six against the better anchor, so the effect is not backbone-specific: Weather wins in all three settings, ETTh1 and ETTh2 lose in all three, and ETTm1, ETTm2 and Electricity vary.

Against the stronger anchor that holds on Solar (−8.7% at H=96, −11.2% at H=192, 20 of 20 seeds) and on Traffic (parity, which R(D)=0.14 predicts). We agree with the reviewer on Exchange: the −26.3% we reported over DLinear is level anchoring on data close to a random walk, and nothing more. Against NLinear it is parity at H=96 and behind at H=192, so we withdraw it as a win.

That is a narrower claim than the one we made, and it is one we can stand behind. As P.3 states, the collapse diagnosis and R(D), which are the contribution, do not depend on it. **Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

Thank you for a second careful reading. Putting the two quotations side by side was the right check. We answer the first point below. On the second, you named the control we needed, and we have run it.

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's. We have now measured it.**

The paper is right, and the clause you quote from our W3 answer is wrong. We are grateful for the check, because it sent us to measure something we had only argued about.

We took the exact tensor a hidden-state router reads. That is the mean-pooled last-block hidden state, the input AdaMix's router uses. We then asked how well each window's statistics can be recovered from it.

- Moirai: the mean comes back at R²=0.996, and log σ at 0.961.
- MOMENT with RevIN: −0.311 and 0.600. They do not come back.
- MOMENT with RevIN switched off: 0.999 and 0.951.

The third row is the important one. The encoder is just as deep, so the probe is reading the normalizer, not the depth. §4.1 says non-learnable I/O scaling leaves the (M,Σ) statistics in the hidden states the router reads. That is what we find.

We should also say how the mistake happened. We reasoned about what per-instance scaling does to its own input, and then wrote it as a claim about the representation the encoder builds. Those are not the same thing.

For Moirai the reasoning does not apply at all. We use the frozen encoder as a feature extractor, sending the input straight through its input projection, so no per-instance scaling runs in that path. The statistics reach the router untouched. MOMENT is different, because its RevIN is in the loop, and the RevIN-off row above is what isolates it. §4.1 states the outcome correctly, and the revision will make the path explicit.

This also answers your W3 question: why does raw routing gain 12–29% on a backbone that never collapses? That number compares RR-MoA with the best fixed adapter (Table N.1: ETTh1 −29%, ETTm1 −16%, Weather −12%). So it measures what routing buys where routing is possible. It is not collapse repair, and nothing needs to have gone missing for it. It is also not App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect, because in RR-MoA the raw signal reaches only the router, and the experts read frozen hidden states. We will drop the word "recovery" from that sentence. That word was what implied a loss.

On the two rules, you are right that they are not interchangeable as we wrote them. The fault is in our sentence, not in the paper. Appendix H already states the general criterion in its own words: whether normalization causes or prevents collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal. That is the rule we gave Reviewer 8b2Z. It is the paper's rule, not a replacement for it. The learnable-affine clause in §4.1 is not a second, competing law. It is what separates the normalizers among the backbones we compare, and its consequence for Moirai is the claim we have now measured.

Our own wording last round was worse than either rule, and we withdraw it. Collapse does not need both conditions at once. Proposition 1 gives two separate routes:

1. The backbone is trainable and co-adapts with the leading expert. Raw routing breaks this route by construction (the corollary to Prop. 1).
2. The router's input is made uniform, so the experts can no longer specialize. Prop. 1(ii) names this as what non-collapse still requires once the backbone is frozen.

Appendix H shows each route on its own. The ResNet control has no normalizer at all, yet it collapses under an unfrozen backbone. The ViT control has a frozen backbone and a non-learnable InstanceNorm1d, and it collapses too. Our own frozen AdaMix follows the second route: entropy 0.32–1.00, against 1.48–1.57 with a raw router. Asking for both conditions at once would contradict our own main result. The revision will state the two routes.

Moirai has neither route. The backbone is strictly frozen, and the statistics are present in what the router reads. So §4.1, Appendix H's principle, and our answer to 8b2Z are one account, not three, and that single W3 clause was the only thing out of place.

**2. The anchor control: you are right, and the swap costs us our largest margins.**

We are convinced that both facts you cite are correct, that the inference from them is correct, and that the control you propose is the right test. So we have run it. We trained a from-scratch NLinear under the DLinear anchor's own protocol: Linear(512→96), 49K parameters, same optimizer, same schedule, same splits, n=10 seeds, nine datasets. It differs from the anchor in one thing only, the level shift. In that sweep our DLinear also reproduces the paper's six calibration values (ETTh1 0.4187 against 0.419), so the swap is measured against the baseline the paper used.

We had reported both facts ourselves, in Appendix A and in the Batch-4 analysis. We never put them together. You did, and that reading should have been ours.

The effect is real, and we can now say how far it reaches. NLinear is the stronger anchor on three of the nine datasets, and all three have drifting levels: Exchange (−28.9%), ETTm2 (−7.9%) and ETTh2 (−3.8%, and −19.0% at H=192). On the other six it is equal or worse, and on Traffic it loses every seed. So the swap does not favour one side everywhere. But it is decisive exactly where you said it would be.

What this does to our numbers is the part that matters. On MOMENT-small at H=96, n=10:

- against DLinear: four wins, one parity, one loss (ETTh1), as reported.
- against NLinear: three wins, two parities (ETTh1 and ETTm1, both inside 0.1%), one loss (ETTh2).
- against the better of the two anchors on each dataset: **three wins out of six**, on ETTm2 (−3.2%), Electricity (−1.6%) and Weather (−4.9%).

The two largest margins we quoted are the ones that go, because ETTh2 and ETTm2 lose most of their gap to level anchoring. You are right that best-of-anchor is the number to lead with, and the revision will lead with it.

We have since run the same control on MOMENT-large, on Moirai, and at H=192 (n=3 each). Each lands at three of six against the better anchor, so the effect is not specific to one backbone. Weather wins in all three settings, ETTh1 and ETTh2 lose in all three, and ETTm1, ETTm2 and Electricity vary.

Off the six, our W4 answer said the recipe generalizes to new data without re-tuning. Against the stronger anchor that still holds on Solar (−8.7% at H=96, −11.2% at H=192, 20 of 20 seeds) and on Traffic (parity, which R(D)=0.14 predicts). We agree with you on Exchange. The −26.3% we reported over DLinear is level anchoring on data close to a random walk, and nothing more. Against NLinear it is parity at H=96 and behind at H=192, so we withdraw it as a win.

Your second point deserves a direct answer: as reported, the grid cannot tell "the backbone adds value" apart from "NLinear beats a simplified DLinear". We think it reaches further than you stated. Beating NLinear would not have separated the two either, because Residual-IA+ also differs from a from-scratch anchor in its training schedule. What does separate them is closing the residual gate, which leaves the shared NLinear branch and nothing else. We ran that too: six datasets × three seeds × H∈{96,192,336,720}, same recipe, same seed, same split, with the backbone as the only variable. The frozen backbone helps on Weather at every horizon (−3.1% to −4.4%). It is close to neutral on ETTm1. It costs on the other four. Pooled over the 72 matched pairs, it costs 2.7%.

That retracts a claim from our first response, and we would rather say so than leave it standing. Our W4 answer had two halves. The first half was right: at H=96 the backbone's contribution is dataset-dependent and small on average, which is what Appendix P.3 says in its own words. The second half, that the backbone is decisive at H≥192, was not. It rested on the backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE, and that model replaces the raw branch as well as removing the backbone, so it never isolated the backbone. The matched toggle does not support the claim at any horizon.

What survives is P.3's own reading: the frozen backbone helps where the dynamics are nonlinear, and adds nothing where a linear model is already close to optimal. P.3 also reports the one backbone effect the toggle does not touch. With the backbone present, the same gate, on the same raw input, routes more sharply (mean entropy 1.34, against 1.49 without it). That is a statement about routing, which is what the paper is about.

For the revision we will name the anchor as the undecomposed single-Linear variant of Zeng et al., wherever the 65:11 count and the abstract sentence appear; add the NLinear anchor to the grid and report best-of-anchor counts beside it; and re-scope the Residual-IA+ claim from "matches or beats DLinear" to what this control supports, namely that it beats the better linear anchor where the dynamics are not linear-dominated, and matches it elsewhere.

That is a narrower claim than the one we made, and it is one we can stand behind. As P.3 says, the collapse diagnosis and R(D), which are the contribution, do not depend on it. Both of your readings landed on the load-bearing thing, and the paper is more accurate for them.
